items.title: Jos Verstappen was hyped like Max - until it all went wrong
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
The degree to which Jos Verstappen’s own Formula 1 disappointment fuelled everything he poured into son Max’s preparation for his ultimately-phenomenal F1 career is already part of motorsport folklore.

The element that perhaps gets overlooked now is how good Jos’s own F1 career was supposed to be - that there was a period, a short one admittedly, when there was just as much excitement over Jos’s prospects as a future F1 champion as there was over Max’s arrival on the F1 grid in 2015.

As the latest episode of our new F1 Rewind podcast series with Edd Straw and Mark Hughes explores, it’s a test for Footwork at Estoril in late September 1993 that really starts the hype.

Only two years out of karting, and having just won the German Formula 3 title, 21-year-old Jos sets a time that would’ve put his very middling car 10th on the grid for the previous weekend’s Portuguese Grand Prix. Track evolution played a part in his time, but the impression his overall performance makes is huge. Verstappen gets the cover slot on the next week’s Autosport magazine, which declares him ‘F1’s hottest new boy’.

Edd Straw: “If you look at Jos Verstappen's career record and didn't experience it or live through it, it's really easy to underestimate how big an impact this test really made."

Mark Hughes: “He was a seriously hot property at that time. He came straight in from karting and won championship immediately in GM Lotus in the Benelux Championship. He'd done a one-off guest appearance in the bigger league GM Lotus series at Spa. He was sensational in that.

“He moved straight to Formula 3, won the German championship, dominated it, and looked set to set the F1 tracks alight.

“The teams were falling over themselves trying to get him on a long-term contract. If you were looking for where the next Michael Schumacher or Mika Hakkinen might be, that's where you are looking. No question.”

Edd Straw: “Everybody was talking to him basically. McLaren gave him a test at one stage. Obviously Benetton, who he eventually signed for. There was a little bit of Ferrari interest even. It was an absolute clamour because this was the next mega-star.

“Also because of how rapid his ascent was. Karting to F1 in two years. In recent years we’ve got a bit more used to really fast ascents, such as Max Verstappen’s. But that was really, really rare at this point.

“So you've not only got this driver who is considered to be incredible, but he's on this rocketship to F1 as well.

“And if in late 1993 you were saying, ‘right, who is going to come into F1 and win races and be a future world champion?’ Jos Verstappen is the name people would have picked out.”

Mark Hughes: “Overwhelmingly at that time. There was no question. He was on the verge of something big.”

Verstappen and manager Huub Rothengatter pick Benetton, which is offering a season of testing and preparation in 1994 then a guaranteed race seat - either in its own squad, or placed elsewhere - for 1995.

But rather than getting a year of learning outside the spotlight, Verstappen is thrust into Benetton’s second race seat alongside Michael Schumacher when JJ Lehto is injured in a testing crash.

Verstappen ultimately gets two stints in that seat, with Lehto still struggling on his return and having to step away again, before being benched at the end of the season so Benetton can evaluate Johnny Herbert in that car.

It adds up to 10 of the 16 1994 rounds in the second Benetton, with Verstappen earning two podiums, but also being sent into a terrifying aerial crash on his debut in Brazil in a pile-up triggered by Eddie Irvine and being caught up in the infamous German GP pit fire.

Later admitting he found the Schumacher-centric car “too nervous” for him, Verstappen never outqualified or even once led Schumacher at the end of a racing lap in their eight outings together with a massive 1.920s (2.288%) average deficit.

Going up against Schumacher in the same team as an underprepared rookie, amid a season of turmoil, was a tall order. And it was enough to instantly crush all that career momentum and hype Verstappen had carried into F1.

Mark Hughes: “In hindsight, he wasn't ready, he came in too early. Had the original plan played out, he would have been getting a lot of mileage away from the spotlight of grands prix and would have probably come in much better prepared in 1995.

“Not only that, Benetton was absolutely centred around Michael Schumacher and team boss Flavio Briatore was into driver management and then making money on drivers.

“Rothengatter and Verstappen had unknowingly surrendered control of his own destiny. As well as being in essentially just the second string car in a team that was totally focused around one driver, Verstappen wasn't even going to be in charge of where he was going to go next.”

Edd Straw: “He has this weird season and actually a big chunk of that career momentum's wiped out by that first season. It really, really is. It's not gone. There's still a residual, ‘oh this guy's good’, but already pretty much the die is cast.”

Mark Hughes: “It saps you of energy when you get into a situation like that where you're the second driver and you're not the focus of anything. And you've been used to being at the absolute centre of everything. You've been used to being treated as a megastar in the making and with everything centred around you in the junior category, with everybody there for you, everybody on your side. And suddenly to be in the lackey role, I think it does damage you.

“And not only that, but you're going up against Michael Schumacher as a rookie.

“And in his more reflective later years, Verstappen also said that even disregarding the equipment differences - and there were significant equipment differences at Benetton - and even disregarding all the factors against him, when you looked at some of the things that Michael was able to do close up and suddenly have to say to yourself, ‘I came in thinking I was going to win races, I think I'm going to win the championship, I'm going to beat everybody’ and then you come up against somebody like that and you think, ‘no, maybe I have to recalibrate here’.

“And even Verstappen acknowledges that maybe he wasn't Michael Schumacher.

“But he was pretty good. Better than he was able to show subsequently.”

Watch or listen to F1 Rewind for much more on Jos’s F1 career, including the later big opportunities that fell through, and an in-depth look at how it all fed into the way he handled Max’s upbringing and journey towards F1.

items.title: Searching for a future – The riders still without a contract for 2027
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The transfer market has been in full swing since August, with dozens of riders changing teams all across the peloton, and dozens more extending with their current teams. Many of these deals are done as early as the spring, with other decisions continuing to be made through the summer.

But as the off-season, the winter and the new year rapidly approach, October marks the time when those riders who don’t yet have a contract for next year start to worry.

Deals can be struck late on, yes, but rosters are starting to fill up, and with a few big names still on the market, a lot of teams want to leave themselves some flexibility until the last minute.

For riders, though, that means they can be left scrambling and having to rethink their futures.

At the time of writing, over 120 WorldTour riders don’t have an officially announced contract for 2027, with hundreds more still contractless at the ProTeam level. Some of those may know where they’re going to be racing; it just hasn’t been announced yet, whilst some are still weighing up their options and making a decision, and some are desperately trying to find a spot for 2027.

With rosters rapidly filling up, here are some significant names who are still without an official contract for 2027.

Various outlets and journalists have linked him with several different teams, including Lotto-Intermarché and Tudor, and there are multiple teams in the peloton that would surely be interested in signing the multiple-time Grand Tour winner and current European TT champion. But so far, the 36-year-old hasn’t been officially tied down to any team, and we don’t know where, if anywhere, his signature will land for 2027.

Roglič is in a better position than most, because it seems like he definitely has options on the table – he can certainly continue racing if he wants to – but that doesn’t mean that it’s an easy decision to make. A lot of other deals might be hanging on the outcome of Roglič’s transfer, too, so this is a significant contract to follow at this late point in the window.

Former Giro d’Italia winner Tao Geoghegan Hart has never quite been the same since his crash and severe injuries sustained at the Giro in 2023, and though Lidl-Trek put their faith in him with a three-year contract, he hasn’t been able to rediscover his Grand Tour-winning level since then. Now, six years after he took home the maglia rosa, it’s not clear whether we’ll see him in the peloton at all next year.

Earlier in the year, the prevailing talk around the paddock was that Geoghegan Hart was set for a quiet retirement, but more recently, Daniel Benson has reported that a move to EF Education-EasyPost could be on the cards.

Nothing has been confirmed yet, though, and if a deal hasn’t already been signed, his run of DNFs in the last months won’t have helped in getting something across the line. Geoghegan Hart was once one of the best riders of his generation, but will now likely take a pay cut at the very least, if he does want to continue in the peloton.

Lucinda Brand recently confirmed her exit from Lidl-Trek, opting to stay with Baloise Verzekeringen–Het Poetsbureau Lions cyclo-cross but giving an answer about her future on the road. In an Instagram post at the time, she suggested there was news coming on that subject, so it seems likely that she does indeed have a road contract for 2027, but it’s yet to be announced.

An extremely experience and successful racer who is clearly still firing on all cylinders, it seems unlikely that Brand would struggle to find a spot for 2027, but the fact that nothing has been announced yet could point to her looking wider than the WorldTour for her future.

After nine seasons in the WorldTour, James Knox may be facing the end of the road this season as he has struggled to find a new team, with no extension forthcoming at Picnic PostNL after the expiry of his one-year contract.

"Of course I wish I did have something," he told at Il Lombardia. "I would still cross my fingers, but the reality of the situation with cycling now, with limited space for the WorldTour teams, many, many quality riders, a lot of focus on points, and younger riders coming through with guaranteed contracts from development teams… I think it's become a situation where it might be hard for me to get anything for next year. I don’t know what will come of it."

Though not a prolific winner himself, Knox has established himself as a dependable climbing domestique, but that's perhaps one of most competitive areas on the transfer market, and as a result, it might be a premature end to his road career this winter.

Gaia Realini agreed to depart Lidl-Trek this year despite having a year left on her contract, and whilst she reportedly has interest from other teams, nothing is confirmed yet, and we're still waiting to hear the exact details of her future.

Often, if riders are leaving teams early, it's because they have a better offer somewhere else already, but it's not always as clear-cut as that. Sometimes things simply aren't working out, or the team want to free up space to bring in another rider by striking a deal with an existing one to leave early, so such an exit doesn't always mean that something else is already lined up.

A talented climber with plenty of potential, Realini seems primed to find a new home, but we'll wait to see where.

Belgian veteran Tom Van Asbroeck is a mainstay of the professional peloton, and the winner of Classics like Binche-Chimay-Binche as well as a respected Classics road captain, but at 36 he’s joining the legion of older riders who would like to continue their careers, but struggle to find a spot to do so.

Van Asbroeck told that he was expecting his contract to be renewed for 2027, but things changed when NSN received "an opportunity the team couldn't pass up" and his future with the team came at the expense of a new signing.

"I hope for the team's sake that they have made the right decision, but it leaves me with a bitter feeling," he said. "It is strange that I was deemed good enough for a Tour selection and numerous major races, but now there is suddenly no place for me anymore. That is contradictory and particularly confronting."

At the other end of the spectrum from Van Asbroeck, there are riders who are only just starting their careers but find themselves faced with an early hurdle of not having a team. This seems to be the situation facing France's Alexy Faure Prost, who joined Picnic PostNL this year but is facing retirement at only 22.

"There's only one step between being among the world's best in your category, being courted by the biggest teams, and being forgotten while being even stronger than before," his girlfriend wrote in an Instagram post that Faure Prost collaborated with.

"Finding another contract back or simply renewing for another year on the same team is becoming more and more impossible. No, ending a professional career at 22 is not normal. Behind all the training data and contract money, there is always a human, not a robot."

Will professional sport understand one day that taking young people from junior ranks to the highest level is also about accompanying them? Not just putting them in races. I sincerely hope that a team gets this message and that it's way too early for you to stop showing your talent."

Neo-pros must be given a minimum of two years on their first contract, but after that, many face uncertain futures and the harsh reality of the world of future talent, where if you don't prove yourself at a young age, you might not be able to continue at all.

As the chances of finding a contract get narrower and narrower, many riders have started to come to terms with the fact that this may be the end of the road for them, and have started sharing their stories on social media. Asbjørn Hellemose did that over the weekend, confirming he won't be continuing with Jayco AlUla next year.

"With how the transfer market looks at the moment, I will most likely not continue as a WorldTour rider at all," the 27-year-old Dane wrote on Instagram after Lombardia.

"At the moment, I’m not sure what’s next for me. When the season is over, I will have time to sit down calmly and reflect on what the best next step for me will be. What I do know is that I’m extremely proud of what I have achieved with my talent and a lot of hard work. Four years in the WorldTour, with participation in one Grand Tour, one World Championships and four Monuments as some of the highlights. Who would have thought that when I was still a teenager living in Denmark?"

Hellemose's situation is far from unique, and is a sad one where riders don't get the heartfelt send-off that other retiring (by choice) riders did at races like Il Lombardia and Paris-Tours, but are forced out of the professional peloton when they feel they still have more to give.

With well over 100 WorldTour riders still not officially confirmed on teams for 2027, and plenty of squads still with roster spots open for next year, the transfer market is still very much alive, even if it feels like we've seen lots of moves already. There are still plenty more to come, and dozens of riders we could put on our list. Here are a few more:

  • Netcompany Ineos traditionally announce their signings and renewals quite late on, but they have a number of riders out of contract: , and are among them
  • There are question marks over what's next for , as the Irish sprinter hasn't been confirmed as staying with UAE Team L'Imad, despite being one of the few names to challenge Lorena Wiebes this season. Given her talent, it seems more likely that she's shopping around, rather than struggling for a spot
  • 's contract with Decathlon CMA CGM expires this year, and was tight-lipped when asked him about his future at the World Championships

Whilst the lists above highlight riders who may still be trying to nail down a contract at this time of year, there are plenty of riders who don't officially have a contract announced for 2027 yet, but that doesn't mean they're in difficulty. Here's a few of the names on that list and what we know about their futures.

  • will stay with Netcompany Ineos next year
  • is likely to return to her US racing roots and ride for Virginia's Blue Ridge-TWENTY28
  • has a contract to stay with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Daniel Benson has reported

That said, there are also plenty of riders without a confirmed spot for 2027 who almost certainly are in the search for survival right now.

  • Human Powered Health and Uno-X Mobility are both full for 2027, with riders like the Pikulik sisters, Kasia Ragusa, Ingvild Gåskjenn and Alberte Greve currently all contractless for next year

items.title: Yankees news: The second base conundrum
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
The Athletic | Chris Kirschner: The Yankees are reportedly unlikely to give Jazz Chisholm Jr. a qualifying offer, and it seems like the second baseman’s time in the Bronx is just about over. That leaves the question: what do the Yankees do at second base? Captain Aaron Judge seems to have his preferred choice, telling reporters after the Yankees’ ALDS exit, “If we were gonna go win the World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team.” Volpe did look comfortable at second after losing his shortstop job to George Lombard Jr., but Volpe’s work with the bat still leaves plenty to be desired. Luis García Jr. is an interesting option; he’s played second before (albeit with terrible defensive metrics), and looked so skilled defensively at first this year that he could convince you his agility and arm strength would play elsewhere on the diamond.

New York Daily News | Peter Sblendorio: There haven’t been many ex-Yankees kicking around postseason, but one former Bomber has figured prominently in Jake Bauers. Bauers played for the club in 2023 and got off to a hot start, hitting a home run in his first game and posting a .899 OPS over his first ten games with the Yankees.

Bauers couldn’t keep it going that year (neither could the Yankees) and New York ended up trading him in the offseason to the Brewers in exchange for minor league outfielder Jace Avina, who is now the Yankees’ No. 24 rated prospect by MLB Pipeline. On the other end, Bauers has blossomed with the Brewers, running an .874 OPS this season and taking home deserved 2026 NLCS MVP honors.

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Hoch delivers his offseason preview for the Yankees, running down some of the big questions. Among them is the aforementioned second base situation, as well as the matter of what to do with Giancarlo Stanton, Austin Wells’ future with the Yankees, and David Bednar’s fate. Unlike Chisholm, Bednar appears likely to receive a qualifying offer, which is slated to come in at about $23 million for the 2027 season.

The Athletic | Tim Britton: The upcoming MLB free agent class is among the worst in recent memory, and The Athletic looked at the last decade of free agent classes with the benefit of hindsight to get a sense of where this group may fall. The lowest-ranked class ends up as 2017, when the top hitters to sign were Yoenis Cespedes, Dexter Fowler, and Ian Desmond, while the top pitchers were Aroldis Chapman, Kenley Jansen, and Rich Hill. The saving grace for the current crop of free agents is a fairly deep group of pitching targets, headlined by Tarik Skubal but backed up by Michael King, Sonny Gray, Kevin Gausman, and Freddy Peralta. That’s somewhat unfortunate news for the Yankees, who nary need an arm but have an offense that could use reinforcements.

items.title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin wins again on stage 5 as Paul Magnier crashes in final kilometre
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Milan Fretin (Cofidis) struck again at the Tour of Guangxi, the Belgian prevailing in a bunch sprint in Yizhou as overall leader Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) crashed in the final kilometre.

As was the case in the previous four stages of the race, stage 5 was always set to come down to a mass sprint finish, and so it proved as the peloton once again raced to finish as one.

The sprint was set up after the break of the day – featuring Patrick Gamper, Jasha Sütterlin (JaycoAlUla), Brandon Rivera (Netcompany Ineos), Baptiste Veistroffer (Lotto-Intermarché), Davide Formolo (Movistar), and Max Walker (EF Education-EasyPost) was caught 14km from the finish.

Magnier, the winner of stages 1 and 4, looked to be the favourite once again, but the Frenchman didn't make the sprint, crashing along with Max Kanter (XDS-Astana) and several others as the peloton raced towards the finish line.

A host of other top sprinters at the race avoided the carnage to contest victory, and it was Arvid de Kleijn (Tudor) who launched the dash for the line. Instead, it was Fretin who came out on top, timing his run just right to beat Matteo Moschetti (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Erlend Blikra (Uno-X Mobility) to the win.

Magnier may not have added to his win tally, but he can rest assured that he'll continue in the race lead after the stage, heading into stage 6 with a 10-second lead over stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL), who was also held up in the crash.

He's unlikely to hold the jersey all the way to the finish on Sunday, however, with the closing stage heading for the race's only uphill finish at Nongla Scenic Spot (3.2km at 7.3%).

items.title: What one image can't show you about Rwanda F1 track
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
If you adapted the saying 'you should never judge a book by its cover' for the world of Formula 1, then tracks should never be deemed successes or failures based solely on rendered images of them.

What can look like nice lines on a bit of paper are no guarantee that a circuit will be good for racing.

Equally, corners that are spectacular and a thrill for drivers - such as Eau Rouge at Spa, the Degners at Suzuka, or even La Monumental at the newer Madring - look simple affairs when just viewed on a screen.

The disparity between the impression a track render can give and what the reality of a track is like when built is a topic that has come up in recent days following the reveal of the layout of the new F1 track in Rwanda.

The single image released of the new Rise Motordrome track near Kigali, which will host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s, drew mixed responses from fans - which was perhaps fuelled by some of the key elements of the layout not being visible.

That inevitably prompted debate about whether the track was going to be any good for overtaking.

After years working on the project, and thousands of laps of it on a simulator, track designer Alex Wurz is enthusiastic about what has been pulled together.

And there are so many details to the circuit, which will feature the greatest elevation change over a lap of the season, that are not possible to pick out from the render, according to Wurz.

"To give you a little flavour, in Turn 2, we are coming downhill with top speed," he tells The Race. "It's 10.8% [gradient] exactly. We're going into a very high compression with 12% banking, and then going 14% uphill, so you will only see sky.

"Towards the end of the corner from the 12% banking we are going to 6%, and then 4%. And in the sim, this feels just like pure joy.

"My favourite section is coming out of the canopy corner over the crest into the lake.

"The timing of it is that you just get light [as the car rises over the crest] and then suddenly you get a 10% compression, and from there you know your mind has to engage into the fast Esses.

"Those are the corners I think should resonate with the fans in the simulator, on your computer games, but hopefully with the big dogs - the F1 drivers themselves."

An emphasis on 'fighting'

As a former F1 driver and Le Mans 24 Hours winner, Wurz knows an awful lot about what makes a top-line track, and what ingredients are needed to help make a good race.

He says it is naive to think that overtaking can ever be guaranteed by a track layout because passing is influenced so much by car regulations, details on the day such as tyre degradation levels, and even whether a frontrunner has made a mess of qualifying.

What he thinks is critical though is to produce a track that allows drivers to "fight" each other, and that can only come from how corners are sequenced.

"We have wide open corners with corner sequences 1/2/3, where it means attack, defend, attack, defend," he says. "Now if I defended too much, I might be overtaken, or I'm so slow that the next guy is catching up. So, it is initiating fighting.

"If it finally is the track where the most overtakes are going to happen, to be honest, that's random. It depends which tyre manufacturer, and what tyre degradation on that day will happen.

"But it's a drivers' and riders' circuit. It's made for overtaking and fighting, and I think it should tick all those boxes."

Wurz has faith that what he has designed will not just be good for fighting, but also be a challenge that drivers enjoy.

"I think it will be an amazing circuit for racing, but equally for the drivers," he said. "If people like comparisons, I don't like them too much, but with red wine, you speak about berries and oak flavours.

"So, if we do the same with tracks, you could compare some of the sections to Spa because of the ups and downs and the speed and the flow. Of course, also Suzuka is one of every driver's favourites, and there's some flavours which you could compare.

"But it's all authentic and bespoke to the topography; it's flowing, it's fast, but we do have, of course, heavy braking areas."

One important element that is shared by a lot of tracks is elevation change, something that pretty much all top-ranking venues have.

The 197 metres of elevation that the Rwanda layout boasts should deliver something that will make even the straights spectacular, and was not obvious from the render - which The Race has subsequently produced more of.

The back straight for example, which was actually hidden from the images, plunges downhill before a proper compression as it rises up again into a heavy braking area.

There are also complex braking areas that are being built. "On the render, you don't see the long straight well, and you don't see the hairpins," says Wurz.

Effort has gone into creating tight turns with combined braking/turning where drivers are exposed to greater risks of getting things wrong - and therefore being attacked from behind.

"What is really challenging is if you are combining forces: your braking, your turning, to then optimise all four contact patches at the right slip angle," says Wurz.

"So those corners where you arrive at 300km/h and you break down to something like 80km/h or 100km/h, but with long combined phases, they are the ones where you can do the real divebombs. And we have three of those.

"I think those will be the sneaky overtakes. And if you start to defend, again, then your next straight line will be three and a half to four tenths down. And that triggers the fighting.

"And if there is no overtaking from that, triggering the fighting means someone else is coming. So I think it should at least initiate great fighting."

Wurz has consulted a lot of driver friends with ideas for the layout, and says that feedback has been positive.

While he has not identified those he has consulted, he says that drivers with a total of 12 FIA world championships have been involved. As chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, the likelihood is that some of those titles were from F1.

Wurz thinks that, in order to make a layout a good drivers' circuit, it is critical that drivers have input on what works.

"I am in almost everyday contact with the greatest champions of current times, so I do show them tracks," he says. "I do listen to what is said about corner sections and which are rewarding and not rewarding.

"They always have some tips, but the principle layout was seen by one guy who texted me back he said: 'That will be instantly one of the most classic favourite circuits of all drivers.' And I really hope so because it is a lot of work!"

And if you want a hint of the way that the track layout has been shaped by thinking about the challenge drivers face, then there is no better example than the Esses section at the end of the lap.

Wurz says this area, which looks similar to but is not a carbon copy of the Suzuka Esses, is one that is going to punish greedy drivers who try to attack it too much.

"If you get one element wrong, the next five or six corners are off," he says. "That's havoc in your brain, but it's joy if you manage it.

"You are coming around the lake out of the forest corner, which is a really cool corner because it's only forest and the track, and then you come over a hill into a double right-hander.

"Here the lift in the stomach should be perfectly timed to then get the compression on the apex. And from this moment on, every movement you do on your instruments are important: steering, throttle and brake.

"None of the corners are flat. Everything has to be either just a downshift or dab on the brake. You really need to flow from one to the next.

"If you do a little mistake, it's designed that greed is penalising you. And this is so cool for the drivers because you kind of have to hold back a little bit, but you want to exceed it.

"If you slide half a metre too wide, that means you have already 0.15 seconds gone, so you have to be true to yourself. And this is a type of mind game.

"Suzuka does it very well. That's why all the drivers love it, and hopefully we can be in the same category of racetrack as the great ones."

items.title: Sean Kelly: Here’s Why Pogačar Doesn’t Have to Fear Seixas Anytime Soon
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Paul Seixas ended his season with a stunning Il Lombardia win, yet Kelly feels Tadej Pogačar’s reign is secure. For now at least.
items.lbText:
Paul Seixas is seen as a likely successor to Tadej Pogačar. (Photo: Maarten Straetemans / Belga / AFP) (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS)

Paul Seixas has made remarkable progress this season, notching up eight wins in all, including a Tadej Pogačar -type dominance of Il Lombardia last weekend.

However although Seixas’ Cannibalesque ascent of the Civiglio saw him break the record Pogačar set four years ago on the same climb, and despite a stunning rate of improvement this season, experienced cycling analyst Sean Kelly feels the world number one shouldn’t lose sleep anytime soon.

Kelly spoke to Velo this week about the two riders and explained why he is believes Pogačar will have the edge for some time yet.

“If you had Pogačar there on Saturday, Seixas probably would have been able to stay with him once again,” he said, speaking of the hilly finale of Il Lombardia. “But then in the flat sprint he doesn’t have any chance, because Pogačar is very fast in a two-up sprint or a little group sprint.

“It’s the other quality that he’s got. As I said many times, Pogačar can do fecking everything.”

Seixas turned heads in Liège-Bastogne-Liège when the then 19-year-old was the only rider able to hold onto Pogačar when the UAE Emirates-XRG rider went all out on La Redoute.

He stayed with him to the summit and then began trading pulls with him afterward. The duo continued together out front until the defending champion put in a last-gasp surge on the climb of La Roche aux Faucons. That finally broke Seixas, but Pogačar admitted afterward that he had believed they’d reach the finish line together.

It’s incredibly rare for any rider to be able to cling on when Pogačar is going all out on a tough climb. It was an even more remarkable achievement for a 19-year-old second-year professional, and it highlighted the extraordinary talent the Frenchman has.

But Kelly insists that even if Seixas is able to remain with Pogačar, that’s only one part of the game.

“There’s no weakness with him where you can say, ‘oh yeah, we can get him on that one.’ They’re just not there. So I don’t think Pogačar is going to be worried.”

There will be some who will disagree with Kelly’s point. They will point to the large age gap between the two riders, a full eight years. They will note that Pogačar has just turned 28, an age when riders are in their prime, and note that it’s very often the time where performances start to plateau and then, a year or two later, start to decline.

Still, Kelly doesn’t think that will be an issue anytime soon. He argues Pogačar will remain the best rider in the sport as long as one thing is in place: motivation.

“Pogačar at 28, 29 or 30 – if mentally he’s hungry enough to do it, I don’t think there’s going to be a problem age-wise,” the former world number one said. “Pogačar definitely has another three or four top years left in him. But will he do four years? Will he have that focus, the mentality to continue on?

“We hear about these long term contracts and that, but in three years’ time, if Pogačar said after the Tour de France, ‘I’m finished, that’s it, I’m stopping at the end of this year,’ it wouldn’t surprise me.”

Pogačar’s ability to stay at the top level is one vital element in any speculation about their future tussles.

The other relates to the Frenchman himself. Kelly acknowledged that Seixas is forging new ground, being the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and also becoming the youngest rider to start the Tour de France in 89 years.

Those kinds of performances, plus Seixas’ stunning rate of improvement this year—remember, he had no pro wins at all prior to 2025, and now he has eight—lead many to assume that he will leap up another level in 2027.

Hold on, says Kelly. It’s not necessarily accurate to make such presumptions.

“It depends now where Seixas goes from here,” he explained. “Will he continue on improving? Is there much more improvement left in him? Or is he a very early developer, and the level he’s at now is pretty much the level he’s going to be at?

“Maybe that is going to be his best level.”

It seems unlikely that a talented young rider could stop improving, but Kelly believes an error was made this year. He explains what that was and how he thinks it might affect cycling’s most exciting young rider.

“I would be concerned that it was too young to do a Tour de France this year,” he said. “And also to ride it as he did, going for the general classification, every day being there in the battle. His potential might suffer because of doing the Tour de France too young.

“I would be concerned that a guy at 19, doing a Tour of France [as intensely] as they do it now, it could affect his performance next year, the year after. He mightn’t get that potential that would be there if he had been taken along at an easier level.”

Kelly mentions Laurent Fignon as a rider from his era who was incredibly good very young. The Frenchman won the Tour at 22 and 23 but, despite those incredible early performances, never won the race again. He missed out by eight seconds to Greg LeMond in 1989 and won the Giro that same year, but it’s fair to say that his early momentum didn’t lead to the dominance many had predicted.

To be clear, Kelly is wowed by Seixas. He does suggest that slightly sub-par performances by Isaac del Toro and Remco Evenepoel in Il Lombardia made the Frenchman look even better than he was but, nevertheless, he applauds his performance.

He also gives credit where credit is due for the year as a whole.

“You couldn’t but be impressed about the performances. We were hearing about the power outputs that he was doing in training,” he said. “We were hearing all that and then he comes to Pays Basques, the way he dominated there.

“The way he dominated the beginning of the year, that confirmed what we were hearing, what the French were talking him up about. And he’s confirmed all that through the year.…

items.title: The Best Pro Cyclists’ FTPs Are Even Higher Than You Thought
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: We compare the FTPs of Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, and more.
items.lbText:
When Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney won atop Mont Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes this summer, we thought it was one of the best climbing performances in cycling history . Since then, more information has come out, not only confirming Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance, but putting it on the pedestal as the greatest climb in the history of women’s cycling.

We estimated Niewiadoma-Phinney’s output at 5.3w/kg for the duration of Mont Ventoux. But in a social media post, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s husband, Taylor, said that the actual output was closer to 5.6w/kg. This is due to the fact that Niewiadoma-Phinney rode into a headwind in the final third of the climb, and that her raw power output is relatively low, making her power-to-weight ratio even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney is one of a small group of riders in the women’s pro peloton who can probably hold 6w/kg for 10-20 minutes. These types of numbers were unfathomable a few years ago, but just like the men’s side of the sport, we have seen professional cycling progressing at a rapid rate. Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance on Mont Ventoux was one of those moments where we had to rewrite the power curve for women’s cycling. If you could hold 5w/kg for an hour in 2025, you could fight for the podium at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift. But in 2026, 5w/kg won’t even put you in the top five.

In this article, we’ll lay out the best women’s riders’ FTPs, and explain why it is their strength or weakness. Let’s start with none other than the Tour de France Femmes and world championship winner.

The last time that Demi Vollering posted power data publicly was in 2022, but her file from the 2021 Liège-Bastogne-Liège Femmes is still on Strava. The Dutchwoman pushed 362w (6.3w/kg) for 4min 34sec on La Redoute, and went on to take the win in a small group sprint. Since then, Vollering’s power data has disappeared, but we can make some educated guesses as to how much she’s improved.

Vollering finished second on Mont Ventoux, 1:16 behind Niewiadoma-Phinney in the queen stage of the TDFF. But she had attacked on the bottom slopes of the climb, pushing the pace and inadvertently setting up a perfect counterattack for Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering and Marlen Reusser were nearly two minutes behind Niewiadoma-Phinney with a few kilometers to go, but then Vollering put in a massive attack to close the gap by more than 30 seconds. That kind of acceleration is only possible when you’ve been riding well under threshold, suggesting that Vollering had plenty left in the tank while Niewiadoma-Phinney rode away solo.

Despite only pushing an estimated 5.1w/kg for the majority of Mont Ventoux, Vollering finished with such a burst that her actual FTP must be significantly higher. Based on our calculations, Vollering has an FTP of just over 300w, putting her at 5.3w/kg at an estimated weight of 57kg. That means that Vollering has a fantastic balance between raw power and w/kg. It’s why she can drop most riders on a climb, but she can also drop them on a shallow descent. She can solo to victory on the flats, and win a small group sprint with her raw power output. For her biggest rival at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, it is a completely different story.

At an estimated 49kg, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney is about 8kg lighter than Vollering, and more than 20kg lighter than Marlen Reusser. That creates a massive raw power discrepancy between the rivals, with few scenarios in Niewiadoma-Phinney’s favor. One of the only times that Niewiadoma-Phinney has the upper hand is on steep climbs. We saw this at the TDFF, when Niewiadoma-Phinney broke away on Mont Ventoux, and was able to follow Vollering’s attacks on a number of short and punchy climbs.

But as soon as they reach the descent or flat section of road, Niewiadoma-Phinney is immediately disadvantaged. We saw this clearly on stages 8 and 9 of this year’s Tour de France Femmes. Niewiadoma-Phinney was only a few seconds behind Vollering at the crest of a key climb, but then she would lose 20-30 seconds on the descent. These were shallow, non-technical descents of 3-5%, meaning that raw power and high speed would dominate.

But on the long and steep climb to Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio reigned supreme. The Pole broke away on the steepest section of the climb, building an insurmountable lead before the shallower and windier section of the course. At 49kg, she was giving away 50-100w compared to Vollering and Reusser, but that didn’t matter on a 9% gradient.

Niewiadoma-Phinney likely has the highest FTP in terms of watts per kilogram in women’s cycling. She reportedly did 5.6w/kg for 55 minutes on Mont Ventoux, which means her fresh numbers could be even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney – Mont Ventoux (UPDATED)

Steep Section to Chalet Reynard : 32:09 at 5.7w/kg (1,540 Vm/h)

In stark contrast to Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio is Marlen Reusser, one of the tallest and most powerful women in professional cycling. Standing at 1.8 meters tall, the Swiss rider weighs an estimated 70kg, meaning that she has more raw power than perhaps any other woman in the world. In fact, her estimated FTP of 370w is world class, regardless of gender.

Reusser was in the shape of her life at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, and she was riding into a podium spot before a final stage collapse in Nice. But before that, Reusser was following Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney on every piece of terrain. Short climbs, long climbs, technical descents, flats, and final sprints…Reusser was there every step of the way. She even won the 21-kilometer time trial in Dijon, putting 18 seconds into Vollering and over a minute into Niewiadoma-Phinney.…

We are in Arkansas for the last big gravel race of the year at Big Sugar ! While the season is winding down, gravel tech is hot as ever with tons of bikes released late this summer. We caught up with four riders riding four of those new releases to learn more.

items.title: Evaluating Yankees manager Aaron Boone’s 2026 season
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
Some would say that 2026 was a tumultuous season for the Yankees’ skipper, and there is a lot to be said about what went right in Aaron Boone’s decision-making and what eventually backfired to catalyze disaster.

There are many occasions when Boone stepped in at the right time to pull a pitcher and allowed the players to control their own destiny from the plate. He is most confident when he’s defending his guys from the dugout and isn’t afraid to get in an umpire’s face after a bad call. This has always been Boone’s style, and he continued his fiery streak this season with five ejections during regular season games. However, as manager, he is mandated to take accountability for some of the questionable decisions that may have put the Yankees in tougher situations.

MLB insiders Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman recently invited Joe Girardi to assess Boone’s decisions, and the former Yankees manager had a lot of positive takeaways despite a disappointing end to this season. Girardi even went on to claim that this was Boone’s best year of managing in his nine years on the job.

To give him credit, Boone had to navigate through several injuries this season and consistently found ways to keep the Yankees fighting for a playoff spot when all seemed lost, especially without Aaron Judge. Along with the Yankees captain, several star players had lengthy stints on the injured list, including Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Ryan Weathers, and Giancarlo Stanton. Expected 2026 contributors Cody Bellinger, Austin Wells, Trent Grisham, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. all missed a few weeks, too. Despite all the setbacks, Boone still found a way to propel the Yankees to their third conseuctive season of at least 93 wins, and he could’ve matched the 94 from both 2024 and 2025 had a rainout not nixed Game 162.

Contrast this to 2023, when Judge also missed a bunch of time and the Yankees struggled to 82 wins, their worst year in over two decades. Although the personnel may have just been better this time around, Boone did help keep the season from falling apart and rendering September irrelevant (let alone October). Credit Boone and pitching coach Matt Blake for helping the bullpen beat preseason expectations as well; others might not have had the confidence in unheralded names like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, but they had strong seasons setting up for closer David Bednar.

The Yankees skipper also deserves some praise for refusing to put Judge in a spot where he could put his future career at risk. After being sidelined for the final stretch of the regular season with a moderate grade right calf strain, Judge was eager to get back into the lineup as the Yankees prepared for the postseason. Boone and general manager Brian Cashman ultimately decided to leave him off the roster for the Wild Card Series against Boston, which didn’t end up being an issue as the Yankees scored a combined 18 runs in the two-game dusting.

The Division Series was an entirely different scenario. On the advice of the Yankees’ medical staff, Judge was again absent from the series, in which the first two games were played on the turf at Tropicana Field. Judge, much like the rest of the Yankees’ offense, struggled to put up big numbers in Tampa Bay and went a combined 2-for-10 with a home run, four RBIs, and four strikeouts this season. He appeared disgruntled at Boone’s decision to keep him off the field for the series, but it may have been the best choice to allow him more time to recover from the calf injury and not put his career at risk — after all, severe Achilles injuries have been linked to the soleus muscle, which is where his calf was strained.

On the other hand, one of Boone’s most glaringly disappointing choices was putting Grisham in a leadoff spot in an elimination game when the Yankees were at risk of getting swept by the Rays on their own turf. Grisham, who barely saw any action in September, was the last of the batters left to keep the fight alive down 4-3 in the bottom of the ninth. With the hottest hitter of the postseason on deck in Ben Rice—who had been batting leadoff—Grisham ended up striking out in four pitches from Bryan Baker, allowing Tampa Bay to celebrate advancing to the ALCS from the Bronx clubhouse once again. With Grisham putting the cherry on top of an embarrassing postseason performance, the Yankees also continued their postseason losing streak and remain winless on the road since the 2024 ALCS against the Guardians.

It looks like Boone is here to stay for at least another year, as his contract runs through the end of 2027. Hopefully the Yankees can make enough clever moves during this expectedly elongated offseason to put them in a better spot for next season.
