items.title: The Knicks don’t have to trade anyone to keep James Wiseman and Bruce Brown
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
What I’m about to tell you might blow your mind. Hell, it might’ve blown my mind if I told myself this yesterday.

The Knicks are currently facing a roster dilemma. They have 13 players on standard contracts, two below the maximum and one below the minimum.

They have two veterans on Exhibit 10 contracts that they want to roster, Bruce Brown and James Wiseman, but they can only roster one and stay beneath the second apron, something that James Dolan has made clear is a hard cap for the team.

Brown and Wiseman are different players and represent different things. They rose from a ragtag group of veterans fighting for that 14th roster spot, so much so that the Knicks are doing everything they can to keep both. It’s a dilemma we saw last year with Malcolm Brogdon and Landry Shamet before the former retired to make the decision easy.

Wiseman is considered the heavy favorite, to the point where Ian Begley called him a lock. At that point, it would be about trying to find a spot for Brown in a tough environment.

To keep both and stay within Dolan’s mandate, they will need to trade someone. The prevailing candidate has been third-year player Pacôme Dadiet, who is buried on the depth chart and running out of time to prove himself as a player. He’s likely on an expiring contract due to his team option almost certainly being declined by the end of October, but his value is still low enough that he’s a negative asset.

That has caused the team to shop the more productive reserve point guard Tyler Kolek, but such a move would leave the Knicks much more vulnerable in case of an injury to a lead ballhandler. It’s a tricky dilemma.

There are multiple ways that Leon Rose and company can try to sort this out, but there’s one that I recently discovered that would require some extreme savviness and careful day-to-day management.

The Knicks can retain both Wiseman and Brown into Opening Night without a trade. It’s risky, but could be worth it.

The Knicks have two open roster spots, so just from simple roster management, they are allowed to sign both. Further, they are not hard-capped at the second apron, which allows them to exceed it.

The problem, as we all know, is that signing both would push the team over the second apron. While a change of heart is always possible, it would be idiotic and a very bad look if they exceeded it for Brown and not homegrown fan favorite Mitchell Robinson.

But what if I told you that the Knicks can temporarily exceed the second apron with extremely little penalty?

The punishments that come with the second apron are two-sided. They not only impact your trade flexibility but also harm your future. As a first-apron team, the Knicks are already restricted from doing certain things, but here are the things they cannot do as a second-apron team that they can currently do:

  • Using any portion of the taxpayer mid-level exception
  • Aggregating two or more player salaries in a trade.
  • Sending out cash as part of a trade.
  • Acquiring a player as part of a sign-and-trade (think why Denver got nobody back for Peyton Watson)
  • Acquiring a player via trade using a traded player exception if that TPE was generated by sending out a player via sign-and-trade.
  • A first-round pick seven years in advance is “frozen” and cannot be used in a transaction. This cannot be undone unless three of the following four seasons are spent beneath the second apron.

Looking at these restrictions, most of them apply to the offseason. The only ones that impact the Knicks in-season are aggregating salary in a trade, sending out cash as part of a trade, and, most crucially, the freezing of their 2033 first-round pick.

To me, the implications on future draft picks are the biggest reason you don’t want to be in the second apron. If the Knicks exceed it, they won’t be able to use the 2033 pick in a trade for at least four years, something that hurts flexibility as you manage salaries and egos. Not to mention that said pick gets thrown back to No. 30 if you’re in the second apron three times in five years.

Where am I going with this? Well, if you read the fine print of the league’s apron policy, you notice one thing in particular.

The first-round pick restriction is only if the team finishes a season in the second apron.

So, as an example, if a team were to exceed the second apron going into the 2026-27 season, but ducked it via trades at the deadline, they would be exempt from that policy.

So for a team that’s perilously close to said apron facing a dilemma… is that worth pursuing?

If the Knicks were not to make a single roster move between now and Opening Night, they would go into the 2026-27 season as a second apron team, exactly $1.625 million over the barrier. That would mean they cannot do any of the trade-related stuff up there, but that’s about it.

It’s from here that Leon has to work his magic.

The simplest way to do this is to bet that you will eventually find a taker for Dadiet or reasonable value for Kolek, allowing you to trade them and shed their salaries off the books. If this happens in one week, two weeks, or three weeks, everything is all good.

NBA rules about salary retention state that, no matter when a player is dealt midseason, their full salary is wiped off the books. That means it can happen as late as the trade deadline, and it would be as if they had never played for the Knicks.

The problem you run into is that the Knicks lose leverage as time goes on. They don’t have much leverage already, with the league knowing their financials, but imagine a situation in February where they’re trying to find someone to take them out of desperation.

To go down this route, the Knicks would have to have confidence that a player could build up midseason trade value, an injury causes a need to open up elsewhere, or current negotiations evolve over weeks and months to make the transaction.

The other route would be to keep Brown and Wiseman on non-guaranteed contracts and watch the clock.

The two currently each have a cap hit of about $2.45 million, which combined is $4.9 million. That means that the Knicks, with no trade made, would need them to make $3.275 million or less combined to stay below the apron. The exact number that each player is able to make this season on the roster concurrently is $1,636,884.

As an example, let’s say Wiseman stays all year. That means he makes $2,449,421, which means that for the Knicks to stay under the second apron (assuming no trades), the max that Brown can make is $812,537. Via the NBA’s prorated salary system, he passes that mark on Black Friday (November 27), so he would need to be cut prior to Thanksgiving to get through waivers.

By doing this, the Knicks would use every last penny they have available to them to maximize their roster and give themselves an extra month to figure out what’s going on. The downside here is that you might get stuck in the same spot of figuring out who to keep, plus you would not be able to sign a 15th player in February, which they can do if they cut Wiseman or Brown this week.

If all of this cap jargon confused you, here’s a TLDR of the two ways the Knicks can go into the season with Wiseman and Brown and no trades:

  • If the Knicks find a taker for Kolek or Dadiet or any way to cut $1.6 million off their books by the trade deadline, they will finish the season beneath the second apron
  • If the Knicks release either Brown or Wiseman by November 27 (more like November 25 due to waiver rules), they will save enough money from the non-guaranteed deals to stay just beneath the second apron

I find these unlikely, just because it’s a very MyGM way of operating and not one you’d see in a league where you need to balance personal relationships with roster building.

But it’s theoretically possible!

items.title: Ranking the Premier League's all-time greatest super subs
items.content: <article>Some players are destined to make their biggest impact off the bench, but who are the top 10 Premier League super subs of all time?</article>
items.lbText:
Mikel Arteta may be attempting to rebrand them "finishers" but there's only one phrase in the footballing lexicon to sum up today's focus: super subs.

Yes, we're looking for those players renowned for making a devastating impact off the bench, those guaranteed game-changers a manager turns to when in desperate need of a goal.

First, an honorary mention for some who missed out, such as one-season wonder Adam le Fondre, who holds the record for the most goals off the bench in a single Premier League campaign - five of his eight came in a three-game spell in January 2013.

Hernan Crespo boasts the best goals-per-game ratio but his six in 16 substitute appearances for Chelsea represents a small sample size, likewise ex-Norwich and Leicester forward Mark Robins with five in 14 outings as a replacement.

To make the all-time top 10 Premier League super subs, players need to have consistently delivered throughout their careers, providing goals and assists.

So here we go, I've ranked mine below - you can have your say in the comments, too.

Theo Walcott, replaced on 168 occasions, holds the record as the most subbed off player in Premier League history. Yet it's his impact coming on to the pitch we're interested in here.

Bursting on to the top-flight scene as an explosive teenager, the flying forward was often used by Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger to stretch defences with his pace and movement - a lactic acid-inducing sight for flailing full-backs.

The England international pieced together an impressive substitute CV throughout his Premier League career.

No-one has more than Walcott's 14 assists as a sub - Ryan Giggs and Marc Albrighton are level - while he also scored 10 goals as a replacement across his time with the Gunners, Everton and Southampton.

It puts him fourth on the list for overall goal contributions off the bench.

This was a toss up between Victor Anichebe and Divock Origi, with both forwards contributing exactly half of all their Premier League goals as a substitute.

Ex- Everton , West Brom and Sunderland striker Anichebe edges it having notched a couple more - a tally of 13 placing the former Nigeria international in joint-eighth on the all-time list - while he also chipped in with five assists off the bench.

Roman Pavlyuchenko was also unlucky to miss out - 45% of his 20 Premier League goals came as a substitute for Tottenham .

There's a good case for Danny Welbeck, who as the only current player in the top three, with 19 goals, still has time to catch those above him.

Welbeck was a goalscoring sub at Manchester United and Arsenal but perfected the art on the south coast, with 12 of his tally coming during six years with Brighton .

The 35-year-old is now at Chelsea but - with apologies to Danny - there is another former Blue whose stats demand a place on this list.

Daniel Sturridge has two fewer substitute goals then Welbeck but has scored a slightly higher percentage of his overall Premier League tally as a sub - 22%.

The former England man, who played for Manchester City , Chelsea , Bolton, Liverpool and West Brom in the top flight, was good for an assist, too.

In fact, when you take his total goal contributions of 24, he provided at a more prolific rate than every substitute in Premier League history - bar Edin Dzeko and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer.

Richarlison matches Sturridge for minutes per goal contribution, but with eight fewer the Brazilian, perhaps harshly, misses out.

A World Cup and Champions League winner, one of the few trophies Olivier Giroud hasn't got his hands on is the Premier League title despite a knack for scoring important goals off the bench.

The Frenchman is second on the all-time substitute scoring list, accounting for 21 of his 90 top-flight goals - that's almost a quarter - with only Dzeko, Solskjaer and Javier Hernandez boasting a better minutes-per-goal record as a sub.

Giroud honed his ability to make a late impact at Arsenal and Chelsea , making 103 substitute appearances in total across 10 seasons in the Premier League.

Good feet for a big man. Tore Andre Flo was a menace for Premier League defenders not merely because of his tall, gangly frame but for the silky touches the Norwegian often showed with his giant boots.

Flo scored 34% of his 38 Premier League goals as a substitute - the eighth-highest ratio for those with 20 top-flight goals or more, while he is also joint-eighth overall for goals from a substitute.

The first of those came just three minutes into his Chelsea debut in 1997, and it was with the Blues he enjoyed his best Premier League output before a later stint at Sunderland .

Having also provided three assists as a sub, he ranks fifth for minutes-per-goal involvements, contributing to his side scoring once every 78 minutes on average when used off the bench.

The Little Pea. Small in stature but a giant headache for tiring defenders.

Of all players in Premier League history to have scored at least 10 goals as a substitute, only one - Sergio Aguero, and it feels a stretch to call the competition's sixth-highest scorer a super sub - has netted at a more prolific rate than Javier 'Chicharito' Hernandez.

He has 19 in 78 sub appearances, a rate of 0.24 per game, with 36% of all his Premier League goals coming after he started on the bench - predominantly for Manchester United but also later in his career at West Ham.

He netted on average every 88 minutes when used as a replacement.

Indeed, only Jermain Defoe and Giroud have scored more goals as a substitute than the Mexican, while he sits among a leading group of seven - including Defoe - who have scored five match-winners as a sub.

Aged 40, Edin Dzeko is still scoring goals for Bundesliga outfit Schalke. His record as a substitute in the Premier League, however, remains among the greatest.

Dzeko netted 50 Premier League goals for Manchester City , with more than a quarter of those coming as a substitute.…

items.title: Evaluating Brian Cashman’s 2026 season
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx.

A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays exposed many harsh realities that are directly tied to Cashman and his decisions.

For the Yankees, 93 wins is not enough. They need to be the best team in the division, because that would bring them additional benefits in postseason play, such as home-field advantage and a ticket straight to the AL Division Series. Everybody in the organization is responsible for how the season plays out, but the spotlight will always point to the head of baseball operations.

Offseason moves and decisions

Cashman didn’t have a particularly bad offseason, but there were some notable holes when the season started. He didn’t find proper replacements for the rehabbing Anthony Volpe and the underwhelming Ryan McMahon: the former ended up being demoted in early August when the organization promoted George Lombard Jr., and the latter posted a 78 wRC+ and just 0.5 fWAR in 124 games. Volpe eventually returned and played an important role in the stretch run and during the postseason.

Extending Trent Grisham a qualifying offer was seen as a moderate risk when it happened, but it was a reasonable one since the outfielder had hit a career-high 34 homers in 2025. The outfielder declined this year, particularly on defense, but at least it wasn’t a long-term commitment.

The trade for Ryan Weathers was universally acclaimed, and it was a good piece of business on Cashman’s part. He ended up posting career-bests in ERA (3.60), fWAR (2.5), and innings pitched (137.1). The executive also brought back Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, Amed Rosario, Paul Goldschmidt, and Cody Bellinger.

Some of them were nice additions, particularly the 2019 NL MVP, but Cashman left the roster exposed to injuries and underperformance in many spots, and that’s on him, too. The bullpen was a bit thin, as some of his past trade experiments, such as Jake Bird, Ángel Chivilli, and Camilo Doval, just didn’t work. The same can be said about Rule 5 pick Cade Winquest. We are more than willing to give Cashman a pass in the bullpen, since the unit finished with the second-best ERA in MLB, though.

Trade Deadline activity (or lack thereof)

The Bombers entered the deadline with a few notable needs, which Cashman was very much aware of. They could have used a catcher given Austin Wells’ season-long slump up to that date, a reliever or two, a starter, and a right-handed outfielder.

They flirted with several backstops, but ended up empty-handed on that front to the frustration of fans. They did bring in Luis García Jr., who had been enjoying an amazing year in Washington with 23 homers and a 133 wRC+.

Heliot Ramos’ arrival was met with mixed reviews, and he posted a disappointing 93 wRC+ in pinstripes. He did have a 184 wRC+ vs. lefties during his time in the Bronx, which was one of the main reasons behind his acquisition. Giving up left-handed pitching prospect Henry Lalane to get him hurt, though. Speaking of…

Yes, you could say that the Yankees’ deadline was a disappointment, although some might disagree. However, they managed to keep most of their top prospects, including Lombard, Dax Kilby, Carlos Lagrange, Elmer Rodríguez, and Ben Hess. The promising Lalane was the lone exception.

They represent, together with Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Weathers, and Will Warren, the next wave of young talent that will, theoretically at least, keep the team highly competitive for the next 3-7 years. Keeping them all, particularly Lombard when half the league was asking for him in trade conversations, was a win for Cashman.

The rest of the farm, however, needs work. A lot of work. The Yankees will need to draft well and be active in the international market in the next couple of years to revamp their depleted system. At least Cashman took a step towards solving the situation, dismissing longtime international scouting director Donny Rowland and replacing him with Mario Garza in January.

Player development wins and losses

As every general manager, Cashman had some player development wins and losses when looking at the final picture of the 2026 campaign. He and his staff managed to turn Blackburn into a very useful reliever with his 1.59 ERA in 85 innings, and he got a nice season from Weathers, too.

Schlittler took a step forward into stardom, and Brent Headrick and Warren also improved in 2026. On the other hand, they couldn’t fix Doval, Luis Gil, McMahon, or Volpe, and Jasson Domínguez remains a fringe player. Grisham and Wells were also subpar for their standard.

The offense, generally speaking, had a mediocre year with a 101 wRC+ that ranked 14th in MLB. Yes, injuries to Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and other key hitters certainly hurt, but the feeling is that Cashman could have done better, or more.

We have said it multiple times in this space: the Yankees need new voices. They need to listen to more prepared people. They can’t keep doing the same things in personnel decisions, player analysis, research and development, and scouting and expect different results. Unless the ownership decides to part ways with their longtime executive, it will be on Cashman to push that change within the organization: does he have that in him, though? It’s at least a fair question.

items.title: I Tested Infinit Nutrition in Death Valley. It’s Worth Full Price.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: I usually wait for a discount to highlight gear, but after two brutal 10-hour days in Death Valley, Infinit’s Custom Mix proved it is worth every penny of full retail.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

My big-ride nutrition strategy is constantly evolving, but when I headed to Death Valley for three 12-hour days on the bike (which turned into two 10-hours days because we were fast then there was a hurricane), I packed a bag of Infinit Nutrition. Sitting at my desk with the trip behind me, I can call it a success. That desert loop was the toughest ride I can remember from a fueling perspective, making Infinit worth putting back on your radar. If you struggle with nutrition on massive days, this could be the answer.

What makes Infinit unique is the custom blend. If you want to get highly specific, you can use a Nix Hydration sensor to measure your sweat composition and use that data to place your order. (I previously wrote a deep dive on pairing the Nix sensor with Infinit if you want the full process). You don’t have to get that technical though. Instead answering a few straight forward questions on the website is enough to build your mix.

For me, the biggest advantage is the sodium control. I prefer to drink my calories rather than eat them, and as a salty sweater, I need serious salt replacement. On long endurance rides, if the sodium ratio is off, I end up desperately thirsty no matter how much water I take in. Infinit allows me to dial in the exact amount of sodium, add a bit of protein, and keep everything easy on the stomach for all-day drinking.

items.title: ‘It’s really not a drama’: Carrick sticks to the script after Martínez storm
items.author: Jamie Jackson
items.content:
Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds

Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds

Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup , and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football , Jason Wilcox.

All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for the former United midfielder.

On the final day of last season, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as head coach.

By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls closed in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.

A game at Leeds in January proved to be Ruben Amorim’s last in charge at Manchester United after he greeted the 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job” . With an uncanny circularity Carrick heads to Elland Road on Sunday after Martínez made similar comments. Amorim’s team were sixth going into that game; Carrick’s start the weekend 13th.

On Friday, though, came a masterclass from Carrick in dialling down emotion as Martínez’s explosive comments about Wilcox – “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director” – were addressed and he repeatedly referred to the “really good feeling” at the club.

“It’s really not a drama for us as a group,” he said. “The boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad … so we’ve moved on pretty quickly.”

If this seems less than credible, and almost certainly a stance coached by United’s PR mandarins, what else would Carrick be expected to say? More obvious was how the zen-like performance required from the club’s leader was being delivered. Even when he broke from the script to interrupt an inquisitor this strengthened the sense of Carrick being in control – hardly easy given the heightened glare on United since Tuesday evening.

When the positive vibes trope was challenged by a questioner saying: “We’ll have to take you at face value”, Carrick’s interjection came with a smile. “I’m telling you the truth when I say that,” he said. “Do you not believe me, no? The players totally believe me. I’m telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while, actually, and that’s it, plain and simple, you know? We’re emotional, we’re passionate, we care a lot.”

When signing on to be the permanent United manager, Carrick had overseen only 21 games at elite level – in two caretaker spells at the club. United had 17 league games to play when he replaced Amorim, and Carrick has shown signs of faltering this season when having to compete on four fronts.

Elimination by Brighton at the earliest stage of the Carabao Cup was not a great calling card regarding an ability to juggle competitions, and there was a surprising reaction from him after the 2-0 opening-day loss at Hull . He bridled at the suggestion United had lacked “passion” during a first-half horror show. “Oh come,” Carrick said. “That’s ridiculous.”

A faulty United rearguard is hampering an attack that is functioning far better and has the most shots (125) and most touches in the opposition box (205) in the Premier League. Nine goals from six matches is not paltry but greater ruthlessness would transform a promising front six into a potent one. Carrick has to find the right blend from Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.

Baleba has sparkled in his first two appearances – against Spurs and Atlético – and might have provided the shield from the No 6 berth to ensure a less leaky defence had he not arrived injured.

This has to be the hope for Carrick. Playing Tielemans at No 10 at Atlético suggests the manager may doubt the 29-year-old’s legs, and questions have been raised about whether United are putting in enough of the hard yards. Their 671.4km distance covered in the league is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2km is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

The trip to an always febrile Elland Road that saves a particular welcome for their cross-Pennines rivals presents a stern challenge. Leeds are ninth and have lost once.

“It’s a great rivalry,” Carrick said, who was full of praise for his Leeds counterpart, Daniel Farke. “There’s big history between the clubs, the areas. That’s what makes these types of games special. You’ve got to embrace the history, what it means.

“I’m sure it will be a fantastic atmosphere on Sunday. It brings an intensity and it’ll be a little bit extra again, on Sunday against us … Of course, we have to be ready, and the boys will be.”

Carrick requires a positive result, though in denying this, he again sounded the right note. “I don’t need results, we all need results,” he said. “It’s not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me, bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this club. It’s not about me, so please …

“I don’t go into every day at work, in this situation, this game, thinking about me. It’s about what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to, and that’s what drives us. So whatever’s best for the club and for the team on Sunday is the most important thing.”

items.title: Verstappen has troubled qualifying in latest GT outing
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Max Verstappen and team-mate Chris Lulham and Ben Barnicoat will start only 15th for the GT World Challenge race at Portimao that Verstappen is contesting in his break between Formula 1 races.

Verstappen's return to the GT scene got off to an eventful start as he tapped Ezequiel Perez Companc's Audi into a spin in a traffic jam on his first lap in morning practice.

Stewards looked at the incident but took no action, and by the end of the second practice session the Verstappen crew was up to fourth.

But they struggled in qualifying, their Mercedes visibly running lower than most and kicking up abundant sparks in the twilight session as they managed only 15th on the 61-car grid.

While Barnicoat called 15th a "could be worse" situation, he admitted the 2 Seas Motorsport-run Verstappen team had taken a wrong turn with the set-up.

"We felt like we'd been missing a little bit of speed - we've been quite high up the timesheets but none of us were super happy," he said.

"So we tried a couple of things there and obviously it didn't quite work out - lots of sparking, a lot of bouncing in a straight line, so I think we just missed it a little bit."

The three-hour race starts at 5pm local time on Saturday. The Boutsen VDS Porsche of Dorian Boccalacci, Morris Schuring and Alessio Picariello starts from pole.

items.title: 'Lemon still has juice to squeeze' - Taylor Phinney clocks new personal best for Individual Pursuit at UCI Track World Championships
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Taylor Phinney’s return to competition at this week’s UCI Track World Championships was much heralded, and while neither he or the US Team Pursuit team managed to take home a medal, Phinney was rightly delighted with his performance in the Individual event held on Friday.

Phinney retired from the professional peloton prematurely in 2019, aged only 29 after a career in which he won 13 races, including a stage of the Giro d’Italia. But while he is perhaps best known as a road rider, he is no stranger to the track, and though the decision to return to international competition might have been a surprise, that he chose the velodrome as the location for that return was not.

Always a powerful rider, he excelled on the track as a younger man, winning the US national Individual Pursuit title aged only 17, before bagging a rainbow jersey winning the same event before his 20th birthday.

Back then, he set a time of 4:16.6 - this week in Shanghai he clocked 4:05.529, a massive improvement on his personal best. Although that was only good enough for eighth place, the now 36-year-old was pleased with his ride.

"Yoooo this one honestly is wild for me to wrap my head around! A PR by nearly 10s in the IP, yes yes positions, technology, etc., but damn, I’m hyped with this one!" he wrote in a post on his Instagram account.

While the Shanghai track hasn’t proved to be a particularly fast one, the Individual Pursuit has produced a new World Record, with eventual rainbow jersey, Jonathan Milan, riding a blistering 3:58.850 in qualifying on Friday morning. While that was significantly faster than Phinney’s time, the American’s ride still exceeded expectations.

"I was hoping to go under 4:10 but once I got out there the vibe was right and the track was ripping. To be top ten with this field is a huge result, something I am super proud of and have worked hard all year for. Felt sooo good to be on my own and tuck up in position and find my rhythm.

"When I saw the start list yesterday and they had me tucked between [Filippo] Ganna and Milan in the first heats I’m not gonna lie I felt some weight on my chest. Even before the start, I had no modern reference for going this fast and competing at this level so I figured it could either go alright or I should be braced for the worst.

"I held steady at 15.0 laps after starting a bit hot and only started to come undone in the last two laps… I’m so inspired for more and beyond grateful to my mentor Tim Decker for getting me back to this point in just 10 months time.

"To watch Jonathan Milan rip a world record right after my ride was cherry on top of the experience for me. To see it done, just after feeling it…I want it all baby let’s go! Lemon still has juice to squeeze."

At the opposite end of his cycling career, Ashlin Barry provided the US team with its best result in the Individual Pursuit, the 19-year-old finishing in fifth in a time of 4:02.304 and providing a fine follow up to his rainbow jersey in the under 23 Road Race at the UCI Road World Championships.

Riding alongside Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson, Barry and Phinney finished seventh in the Team Pursuit earlier in the week, and the country have won only one medal so far, Megan Jastrab finishing third in the women’s Elimination race.

items.title: Driver Who Killed Cyclist Magnus White Denied Parole
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Yeva Smilianska has served a little more than one year of a four-year sentence. She is next eligible for parole in one year.
items.lbText:
Yeva Smilianska, the driver convicted last year of hitting and killing Magnus White , 17, was denied parole yesterday. It was her first opportunity for parole after serving a little more than one year of a four-year sentence.

Smilianska was convicted in June 2025 of reckless vehicular homicide for striking and killing White outside Boulder, Colorado in late July 2023. White, a rising star in the USA Cycling program, had been out on a training ride shortly before he was scheduled to head off to Europe for a block of racing.

The White family believes that had Smilianska been drug tested at the scene, she would have faced a more severe punishment than the four-year sentence she ultimately received.

Smilianska maintained that she was tired after hanging out with friends and called her decision to get behind the wheel “horribly irresponsible” in the parole hearing. She maintains that she only drank a small amount that evening, and did not address evidence from the trial showing that she had been drinking before getting behind the wheel.

Smilianska addressed how her actions have impacted Magnus’ family, though did not mention Magnus’ name, saying “I can’t imagine how they handle all this. I know there’s nothing I can do or say anything. If there were, I would happily do it.”

“I wish I could do anything to help the damage I caused.”

Michael White, Magnus’ father, shared an Instagram post detailing the process of what it was like to listen in on the parole hearing as a family.

“This is what a parole hearing looks like,” he wrote.

“We’re not in a courtroom. We’re not at a prison. We’re in our living room. We haven’t showered. We sit as family, even our dog, and we wait for them to call us.

“At today’s hearing, we heard her speak for the first time ever in a casual, conversational setting. That’s how the interview goes with a parole board member. She didn’t know we were listening in on the hearing. It’s our right as victims.

“After listening to everything she said, it’s clear she STILL doesn’t take responsibility for killing Magnus. She told the parole board member, ‘I was hanging out with a friend, then the car crash happened.’ Then she blamed Magnus’ death on not getting ‘extra sleep.’

“When she was asked about the impact on the victim’s family, she started talking about herself. ‘I’m really struggling about what happened to myself.’ She never said Magnus’ name the entire hearing.”

He went on to thank everyone who wrote an impact statement before the hearing, saying that the Department of Corrections told them the over 500 letters was by far the most they had ever received.

“Today, we can breathe again,” White wrote.

Smilianska is eligible to seek parole again in one year.

The White family started the White Line Foundation with the goal of ending vulnerable road user deaths. Learn more and donate at thewhiteline.org

items.title: Colapinto urges fans to stop online abuse: “You’re not helping me or my future”
Richard Carapaz Breaks Contract with EF Education-EasyPost to Join NSN in Transfer Stunner
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Carapaz and NSN Cycling Team confirm three-year deal that leaves a void at EF and will reshape grand tour racing in 2027.
items.lbText:
Richard Carapaz has split from EF Education-EasyPost to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal that will see him toward retirement.

The bombshell transfer was confirmed Friday afternoon after a wave of speculation following recent reports by Wielerflits .

The 33-year-old had an ongoing contract with the American EF Education-EasyPost team and had enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 season.

He finished top-10 at both the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, and claimed the Tour de France KoM jersey for a second time.

According to Wielerflits , EF Education-EasyPost is suffering a budget pinch going into 2027. The Ecuadorian would have been one of the highest-paid riders on the roster of Jonathan Vaughters’ team.

Carapaz’s exit will be hard felt at EF. He’s been the center of the squad’s ambitions for the past four seasons.

Beyond that, the U.S. team was already reeling from a rider exodus. Five others, including classics talent Kasper Asgreen, have recently confirmed they’re leaving this winter. Asgreen also joins NSN Cycling Team in 2027.

Meanwhile, EF Education-EasyPost has confirmed only one incoming transfer for 2027. Young American Gavin Sherry steps up from the EF-Aevolo devo team.

“Gracias, Richie. Por todo,” EF wrote in a montage video of Carapaz’s greatest hits it posted to Instagram .

NSN Cycling Team heralded Carapaz’s arrival Friday as “a major statement that will strengthen the roster and the team’s grand tour and stage race ambitions.”

The former Giro d’Italia winner and Olympic champion will join Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt in a new climbing division of the Swiss-registered squad.

Having only formed out of the ashes of Israel Premier-Tech at the start of 2026, NSN was focused on sprints with Biniam Girmay and Ethan Vernon in its debut season.

“For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders,” Carapaz said Friday.

“I find the NSN project really interesting. After our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the grand tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for,” Carapaz continued.

“The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together.”

items.title: How Horner, Brown and Wolff made their fortunes from F1
items.author: Darren Cox
items.content:
Christian Horner, Zak Brown and Toto Wolff have been three of the most influential team bosses during Formula 1's extraordinary growth over the past decade.

All three have been very well rewarded for it. But the latest set of F1 team accounts filed in the UK reveal something more interesting than simply how much each has made.

They show three very different ways of sharing in the value that has been created as F1 teams have gone from businesses that often needed wealthy owners to keep funding them to scarce sporting assets now worth billions.

Horner was ultimately a very highly paid employee at Red Bull. Brown has participated in McLaren's growth through a long-term incentive scheme. Wolff owns a significant part of the Mercedes team he runs.

The difference between the three helps explain why ownership now appears to be so important to Horner as he considers what he does next.

Red Bull Technology's 2025 accounts disclose £66.988million in compensation for loss of office for its highest-paid director, understood to be Horner, alongside £9.029m in remuneration.

That puts his disclosed package for the year at around £76m.

Some reports have put the compensation above £100m by adding a separate £33.494m figure contained in Red Bull Racing's accounts. But Red Bull Technology explicitly states that its £66.988m disclosure is for the group, which includes Red Bull Racing. The £33.494m should therefore not be added again.

Even £76m is an extraordinary sum.

But perhaps the most interesting thing about Horner's 20 years at Red Bull isn't what he made. It's what he didn't have: ownership.

That should not be confused with Horner having made a bad deal when he joined Red Bull. Quite the opposite.

At the end of 2004 he was 31, had built a successful Formula 3000 team in Arden, and was trying to find a way into F1. He had looked at buying Jordan but simply didn't have the hundreds of millions required to make the step independently.

Then Dietrich Mateschitz bought Jaguar and turned it into Red Bull Racing.

Horner later recalled being summoned to Salzburg and Mateschitz telling him he had big ambitions for the team and was "willing to take a chance" on him. Horner said he was only 31 and "didn't have to think about it for too long".

And the deal itself wasn't bad either. Horner has since recalled that Mateschitz told him he wouldn't be paid a huge salary but would receive a healthy bonus for every point Red Bull scored. Jaguar had managed nine points the previous season. Red Bull scored 34 in its first.

For a 31-year-old team owner trying to find his way into F1, it was an extraordinary opportunity.

Horner helped turn Red Bull Racing from the remains of Jaguar into one of F1's most successful teams, winning six constructors' championships and eight drivers' titles.

But however well he was rewarded, Horner remained an employee of a business owned by somebody else.

Brown's situation at McLaren is different.

McLaren Racing's accounts show its highest-paid director received £81.897m in 2025, comprising £8.215m in remuneration and £73.682m relating to its long-term incentive scheme. Brown has been identified as that director in reporting of the accounts.

The bulk of the package resulted from an incentive scheme connected to the enormous increase in the value of McLaren Racing.

The turnaround has been remarkable. McLaren was in serious financial trouble during the pandemic and brought outside investment into its racing operation. Five years later, the transaction that consolidated the ownership of McLaren Racing valued the business at around £3.5billion.

Brown therefore had a substantial participation in the increase in McLaren Racing's value through his incentive arrangements, allowing him to share in the upside as the business was transformed.

The comparison with Horner is striking. Both received packages of around £80m in 2025, but they got there in completely different ways.

Horner's was dominated by the compensation he received for leaving the business he had spent two decades building. Brown's was dominated by an incentive designed to give him a share of the value created as McLaren Racing grew.

Wolff's position is different again. Mercedes' accounts disclose £9.528m of total directors' remuneration in 2025, although they don't tell us how much of that was Wolff's individually.

His executive pay is, in any case, almost incidental to the important number. Because Wolff owns the asset.

When INEOS bought into Mercedes' F1 operation, the team was divided equally between Mercedes-Benz, INEOS and Wolff's investment vehicle. Wolff therefore had a one-third economic interest in Mercedes F1 while also serving as its team principal and CEO.

That also allows him to participate in the profits distributed by the business. Mercedes paid £125m in dividends in 2025, meaning a one-third shareholder would have an economic interest in roughly £42m of that if the distribution was made pro rata. That money would, of course, flow through the relevant ownership structures rather than simply appearing as part of Wolff's salary.

But last year provided a much bigger indication of what his original investment has become worth.

Mercedes confirmed the structure but did not disclose the price. The transaction was reported as valuing Mercedes F1 at around $6bn, with Wolff receiving approximately $300m for the stake he sold.

And he only sold 15% of his holding.

Wolff retained the remaining 85%, equivalent to approximately 28.3% of Mercedes F1. At the same $6bn valuation, that stake would be worth around $1.7bn.

That isn't $1.7bn sitting in Wolff's bank account. It is the implied value of a shareholding based on the valuation attached to a minority transaction.

But it shows the enormous difference between being paid to create value and owning the value you create.

Horner spent more than two decades building Red Bull Racing and was extremely well rewarded as an employee, including a remarkable payment when that relationship ended.

Brown helped take McLaren Racing from the edge of a financial crisis to a business valued at around £3.5bn, with an incentive structure that allowed him to participate directly in that increase in value.

Wolff did something different. He bought into the business he was running.

As the value of F1 teams has exploded, that has proved to be the ultimate deal.

Which brings us back to Horner.

Since leaving Red Bull, he has become increasingly clear about wanting something different from the next stage of his career.

His language now is particularly interesting when compared with the 31-year-old who described the original Red Bull opportunity as a "no-brainer".

"I've been a hired hand," Horner said recently. "I did 21 years sitting on the pitwall. I don't need to go back to that."

His preference now is to return as "a partner, rather than just a hired hand".

It isn't difficult to understand why.

The original Red Bull deal was a fantastic one for Horner in 2005. What changed over the following 21 years was F1 itself, and particularly the value of its teams.

F1 teams were once sporting operations that routinely consumed their owners' money. Today, the best of them are global sports businesses worth billions.

If Horner is going to spend the next decade helping to build another one, you can see why this time he appears determined to own a piece of it.

items.title: Carrick brushes off Martínez’s failure to apologise publicly to United director Wilcox
items.author: Jamie Jackson
items.content:
• Manchester United coach accepts defender’s apology

  • ‘He’s realised he’s made a mistake and that’s enough’

Michael Carrick brushed off Lisandro Martínez’s failure to offer Jason Wilcox a public apology after the defender criticised Manchester United’s director of football in the wake of Tuesday’s defeat at Atlético Madrid.

Martínez referred directly to Wilcox after the 2-0 Champions League loss, saying: “I expect more from our technical director.”

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Manchester United coach accepts defender’s apology

‘He’s realised he’s made a mistake and that’s enough’

Michael Carrick brushed off Lisandro Martínez’s failure to offer Jason Wilcox a public apology after the defender criticised Manchester United’s director of football in the wake of Tuesday’s defeat at Atlético Madrid .

Martínez referred directly to Wilcox after the 2-0 Champions League loss, saying: “I expect more from our technical director.”

On Thursday Martínez issued an apology that did not mention Wilcox or withdraw the essence of his outburst: the need for more squad investment. “The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise,” he said.

Carrick was asked whether he respected Martínez for not saying sorry to Wilcox. “He’s released his statement, he’s realised he’s made a mistake and that’s enough for all of us to move on with,” United’s manager said.

Carrick was pressed on whether it would have been better if Martínez had apologised to Wilcox and for his wider comments about investment, rather than just saying sorry for the timing and location of his interview. “From our point of view, the acknowledgment of what’s been done has certainly been enough, we’ve moved on and we’re definitely not looking back at it now,” he replied.

Carrick said Martínez was available for Sunday’s trip to Leeds, where Manchester United go having taken only six points from their opening six league games. They were knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton last month and have one win and a defeat in the Champions League. Poor form has increased the pressure on Carrick, who was asked whether Martínez’s comments were an unwanted distraction that had annoyed him.

“No, I understand emotion at times,” he said. “We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care. There’s a way of doing that, and that’s already been acknowledged, but we need to carry that intensity and that willingness and that togetherness and that spirit. As a group, we need to use it, and we’ve got to use it in the right way.”

Wayne Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, claimed Martínez’s comments “will rip the dressing room apart”. It was put to Carrick that they may have an opposite, unifying effect.

“There’s a lot of things that can affect the group in all sorts of different ways,” said Carrick, who went on to highlight his players’ reaction to conceding inside a minute at Atlético. “It’s one of the toughest places to play in the Champions League, so to go a goal down so early, and the way we responded shows an underlying belief and spirit and a togetherness,” he said.

He indicated that events on and off the pitch this week had brought the squad together. “Certain situations can galvanise the group, and it’s certainly galvanised the group as this week’s progressed. The boys are in a really good place right now.”

Carrick was asked why anyone outside the club, including former players such as Rooney who have criticised Martínez, should believe there is unity. “There’s a lot of people that say a lot of things, and ex-pros or not ex-pros, it doesn’t necessarily mean you understand what’s going on here,” he said. “I’m telling you the truth. The squad today [Friday] was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while.”

Carrick said Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo faced fitness tests.

items.title: Richard Carapaz breaks EF Education-EasyPost contract to sign for NSN
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Richard Carapaz has broken his contract with EF Education-EasyPost early to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal starting in 2027, it was confirmed on Friday.

The 33-year-old Ecuadorian was due to remain on the US team until the end of 2027, but will instead ply his trade at the Swiss-registered squad, bringing "world-class climbing ability, experience, and leadership to the team."

Announced via a social media video with NSN co-founder and Spanish football icon Andres Iniesta, Carapaz is their seventh confirmed new signing for next season. He raced in the pink of EF for four successful seasons, with the US team posting a video of his recent highlights and behind-the-scenes moments with the caption "Gracias, Richie. Por todo."

A former Giro d'Italia winner, Olympic champion, three-time Tour de France stage winner, and winner of multiple Grand Tour King of the Mountains jerseys, Carapaz arrives as a true GC leader for NSN, finishing fourth at the Vuelta a España and eighth overall at the Tour just this past year.

"For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders," said Carapaz.

"I’m simply very excited. I’m really looking forward to it, and to be honest, this reminds me a lot of when I signed my first professional contract, when I was incredibly excited about being in the WorldTour. I still have the same motivation as I did that day and that’s really an incredible feeling.

"I find the NSN project really interesting and after our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the Grand Tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for.

"The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together. I think the team has a lot of potential to develop and I’m excited to be part of that in the next three years."

Carapaz's total haul of UCI points in 2026 was more than double that of NSN's top -ranked rider,

Biniam Girmay, so even into his 30s, he is still among the very best riders in the world and will lead their Grand Tour GC ambitions in the coming three years.

"Signing Richard Carapaz is a significant moment for our team and an important milestone in the development of our sporting project," said General Manager Kjell Carlström.

"Richard is a proven champion. His achievements speak for themselves, but what makes him particularly special is his mentality. Richard is known for his grit and determination, and we saw this shine through in 2026 with his two Tour de France stage wins and the polka dot jersey, followed by an impressive podium a week later in San Sebastián.

"Richard is one of those riders whose passion for cycling is so evident and we believe he still has some of his best performances ahead of him. His experience and leadership will be extremely valuable, not only in helping us achieve our sporting objectives but also in developing the next generation of talent within the team. Richard is someone our young riders can look up to, and I have no doubt he will fit in perfectly in our team culture. We’re excited for Richard’s next chapter at NSN Cycling Team."

Carapaz joins Santiago Buitrago, Lennert Van Eetvelt, Kasper Asgreen, Artem Shmidt and Cedric Beullens as new arrivals for 2027 at NSN. He's also the sixth confirmed departure for

EF Education-EasyPost at the end of the 2026 season.

items.title: Eneco Tour: Mick van Dijke nets maiden pro win as Victor Campenaerts moves into race lead on breathless stage 3
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
After a breathless day of racing, with groups split all over the road, Mick van Dijke (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) took the first professional win of his career from the breakaway on stage 3 of the Eneco Tour in Watersley.

The Dutch rider won ahead of new race leader Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike), after the pair bridged across to the original break in the last 33km, before getting away as the lead duo in the last 18km, and battling out the uphill sprint for the win.

Jonas Rutsch (Lotto Intermarché) and Pierre Thierry (TotalEnergies) survived from the early break to finish third and fourth, with Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) not far behind and jumping up to second overall as a result of his efforts.

Pre-stage race leader Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) tried valiantly to defend the orange jersey, but dropped several times as racing heated up over the undulating Watersley circuit, eventually losing more than a minute and a half and the jersey.

Campenaerts now leads overall by 15 seconds from Mouris, with Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) sat third overall on a 30-second deficit. The orange jersey will be decided this weekend over two punchy stages to the Col du VAM and Arnhem.

"It's the first one. Finally, I'm chasing it already for five and a half years, so I'm super happy," said Van Dijke, then confirming that it was no gift from Campenaerts in the finale, but a result of one rider going for GC and the other the stage win.

"I don't know his name, but the French guy [Thierry] was not pulling anymore, and I said to Campy, 'If he doesn't pull, I won't pull'; then he attacked, and I had to go a little bit deep to catch him, but I managed to."

"We are big friends; Campy was riding for GC, so I was not allowed to pull. I told him that, and if I helped him a little bit, he did most of the work. Then in the end, he went full, and I also went full."

As a tough 110.5km route from Sittard to Watersley welcomed the remaining riders on race day four at the Eneco Tour, a four-rider break found themselves up the road after two laps of the circuit: Rutsch, Thierry, Jesse Kramer (BEAT CC p/b Saxo), and Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam)

With 33km to go, four became seven as Hartthijs de Vries (Unibet Rose Rockets), Van Dijke, and Campenaerts attacked across the gap, with the latter's presence – having started the day just 29 seconds down on Söderqvist – forcing Lidl-Trek to chase in the peloton with two reps of the four hills still to come.

With 30km to go, Soudal-QuickStep started to accelerate, first with Tim Merlier, who was setting up an attack for Pepijn Reinderink. Quickly, Söderqvist found himself going backwards and struggling, but the riders at the front of the peloton began to mark each other as no one was able to get away.

The break started to fracture with the peloton breathing down their necks on the fourth and penultimate time up the Windraak, but the five who remained in front maintained their lead of just under 25 seconds heading into the last lap.

As Söderqvist was fully dropped in the last 20km, struggling to hold the wheels, Campenaerts started making his bid for the overall lead in front, taking the maximum six bonus seconds at the Red Bull KM and then attacking with 18km to go from the break.

Van Dijke was able to go with the Belgian, making it a leading duo in front of the first chase group containing fourth-place on GC Mouris, 21 seconds back, a second group containing Fisher-Black at 43 seconds back, and the peloton containing Söderqvist back at 1:01 heading into the final 10km.

With racing split all over the road, Fisher-Black launched an attack into the last 5.5km, but he was followed by Menno Huising (Visma-Lease a Bike) and the rest of the chasing group he was already in. Soon after, the Kiwi moved across the road and caused Huising – who was looking back at the group – to crash out of the chase.

They made no real impression on the leading duo, though; he entered the final kilometre after Campenaerts had done the lion's share of the work. Van Dijke won the uphill sprint for his maiden success, with the rest of the GC hopefuls coming home behind new orange jersey Campenaerts in dribs and drabs.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘New York will explore other deals this weekend and Monday’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
No more fake basketball for the next eight months, folks!

The Knicks wrapped up the preseason with their most solid performance, defeated the Raps in New York, and will next see the banner(s) rise to the rafters of MSG.

Here’s the latest from everybody and their mothers.

On the Knicks’ progress over the past year heading into their title defense:

“I’m going to keep it real that there’s something in front of us. I’m not a fan of having an elephant in the room. I’ll address it: It’s about the process. It’s not about the end result. We can’t think about the end result right now. We have a ways to go. This is a new season, new team and we’re gonna have challenges in front of us.

“It’s like climbing a mountain. Sometimes you go a 100 yards, but you might get knocked back five yards. Hopefully, it’s not 50 yards, but you might get back five or 10 yards, and you regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way.

“But making sure we embrace the process without slippage in that is going to be huge. And if I see us slipping up, it’s my job to let us know as a team that we’re off track. We need to get back on hopefully sooner than later.”

On why Jalen Brunson is the NBA’s best leader, as voted by GMs:

“He studies the game, and that helps a lot because you can always grow in any field you do. But he walks the talk. He works extremely hard, and he strives for perfection from himself. And when you do that, your peers see you do that, and you’re looked upon as the best player on the team, and it gives you credibility to tell somebody else when they’re not given their all or when they need to do this a little bit better or that a little bit better.”

On Brunson’s toughness and willingness to hold teammates accountable:

“He’s not afraid because, as a leader, sometimes you can be on an island because you have to always be conscious of ‘I got to do more, I got to do more’ in terms of work harder, focus, everybody’s going to make mistakes, but those little things. And so when you tell your teammates, they can get pissed at you, or they can be like, ‘hey, screw him because who is he to tell me what to do?’ And so you have to have some thick skin because it’s not going to always be you telling somebody to do something, then they embrace it. And I think Jalen has that thick skin and a toughness about him to be in a seat like this.”

On Brunson potentially becoming an NBA head coach after his playing career:

“I think Jalen has that thick skin and toughness about him to be in a seat like this. You won’t need to, though. My view? If you don’t want to… It’s up to you, Jalen.”

On what he expects from the Knicks’ final roster spot:

“If one of those guys makes our team, at least right now, they may not even play seven minutes — you know, seven straight minutes. And then at the end of the day, we just have to make a decision.”

On the mentality required from the Knicks’ third-string center:

“We just hope that there’s a passion and an energy and a focus coming from that spot because, I’m sure at times that person will start, at times they may be the first backup and at times they may be second backup. So as the minutes are fluctuating, you’re going to have to generate some internal energy at times, to go play in a low-minute game.

“Sometimes he’ll maybe not play one or two, maybe three games in a row. You look for that, and then you know, you just look for somebody that’s going to play hard at the end of the day – try to do the things that you’re asking on both sides of the floor. And bring a little something different than what the two guys in front of you bring.”

On Bruce Brown’s experience, toughness and versatility:

“Bruce has been through a lot with a lot of different teams at a pretty high level. His toughness, his experience, his feel, all those things — he’s a winner. It seems like every place he’s gone, he’s won, but all those things can add a lot to the program, and then he’s versatile both ends of the floor. He could play a few different positions offensively; he can guard a few different positions defensively. So a guy like that, especially a veteran winner, can be helpful to any team.”

On James Wiseman’s potential and development:

“He’s young, he’s talented, you know, he’s raw, still. I think he’s still trying to establish a foothold in this league. But with the God-given attributes he has, in terms of athleticism and length and quickness, [they] can bode well for him on both ends of the floor. And at 25 years old, he hasn’t even reached his prime, especially knowing he hadn’t played a ton of basketball; having a vertical threat at the rim will help [the Knicks], or could help everybody else play the game a little bit easier, whether it’s driving the basketball or playing pick and roll.”

On his recovery from wrist surgery:

“I had nine different casts. I was able to take it off if I ran or worked out with it. So I had one for workouts, one for showering and obviously one for everyday use.”

On maintaining the Knicks’ championship-winning approach entering a new season:

“I think what’s most important is that last year we took everything one day at a time. We were talking about — obviously, the topic was getting back to the conference finals and trying to advance. And I think for us now, the way we approached it last year was to take it one day at a time, every single day. So not talking about certain things.

“Obviously, we know what it takes, but just going into this with the same mindset for this journey. Even though it’s a new journey, it’s a different journey; the approach has to be the same, if not better.

“The first couple of weeks of the season is going to show us who we are and where we are. No matter what we’re doing, whether we’re playing great, playing bad, how are you going to be able to learn? And so, I mean, we’ll find a way. We’ll hold each other accountable, just like we did last year, and then we’ll be better.”

On the Knicks’ preseason progress and preparing to defend their championship:

“Each game got better and better. Just happy to be back. I feel like it’s a learning experience for us. We have to turn the page on last year and figure out how to get better every single day. It’s gonna be a different journey for us. Our mindset has to be different, and we’ll be ready to go.”

On the Knicks’ preseason finale and preparing for opening night:

“I thought today was a good dress rehearsal. It was cool, it was very nice to get back out there and get back into our flow and be really good. Obviously we have a lot of things to work on. But it was a good way to end the preseason.”

On how he feels physically and his rhythm entering the regular season:

“Yeah, I feel good. I feel really, really good.”

On who’s the biggest complainer to referees among Knicks:

“Josh Hart. Why’d y’all laugh? Did y’all agree with that or something? Everyone behind the camera, I just want y’all to know: y’all just clowned Josh Hart. That’s crazy for y’all to say — in New York, too.”

On choosing between winning another NBA championship and a World Series:

“Win a World Series, for sure. I already won an NBA championship.”

“Before the game starts, I always give everyone at the table, including the fans behind, a chance to really get into the game. Just giving everybody a fist bump down the line of the table, and then go on the court.”

On his favorite all-time big man:

“I think Hakeem. I feel like, in a way, he kind of is mythical, like Wilt Chamberlain… but I’ve been able to talk and meet Hakeem, and he’s an amazing, amazing human.”

On the Knicks’ roster decisions involving Bruce Brown, James Wiseman, Pacome Dadiet and Tyler Kolek:

“Brown and James Wiseman have made it through preseason cuts. The Knicks clearly like both players. But New York only has room under the second apron in team salary to keep one player. In order to keep both Brown and Wiseman, the Knicks would need to trade a player on a standard contract without taking back salary.

“My read heading into the weekend: Wiseman is a lock to make the roster. There is strong support to add Brown as well. The Knicks would need to make a trade by Monday afternoon if they want to keep Brown. I think they will explore all avenues to make that happen.

“It’s logical to assume that the Knicks will move third-year wing Pacome Dadiet. But I believe New York will explore other deals — including trades involving third-year guard Tyler Kolek — this weekend and Monday.

“The Knicks will be asking teams to take on a player without sending back salary. To get a deal done, New York may need to attach its own second-round picks (New York will have at least 11 second-round picks in the next seven drafts).”

On the Knicks’ handling of Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract negotiations:

“So, it was smart to dead the conversation. Now, how you deaded the conversation is the problem. I can’t find out on Twitter if that’s what happened…So if that’s the case (Towns learning from the media that the Knicks paused negotiations), then that’s a communication thing right there. [The Knicks] dropped the ball on that one for one. You don’t let that get outside. So again, I don’t know that. The only thing I’m saying is you don’t break up the family. That’s all I’m going to say. You don’t break up the family.”

On fulfilling his childhood dream of becoming a police officer:

“It’s something I always wanted to do since I was a kid. I remember back when I was in grade school, elementary school. They asked you on career day, ‘What do you want to be when you grow up?’ And my initial response was a police officer.”

On his family’s history in law enforcement:

“It runs in the family. My uncle was a captain. His brother was a deputy. My cousin is a captain. My sister’s in the academy. So, it’s a family tradition, basically.”

On the physical demands of police academy training compared with the NBA:

“Yeah, it was a little bit [more] challenging actually because now I’m running a lot more than I had before. Obviously, in the NBA you run short distances, right? And the police academy, you’re running more long-distance mileage.”

On his wife’s initial concerns about his decision to become a police officer:

“My wife at first was a little bit concerned because obviously being a police officer, there’s some danger to it. But if you are well-trained and you understand your policies and procedures, you’re able to somewhat have officer safety, which is very important, and that’s the goal.”

items.title: 'I am telling you the truth' - Carrick on Martinez fallout
items.content: <article>Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says he is telling the truth about the club moving on from Lisandro Martinez's explosive post-match interview.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says he is "telling the truth" when he says the club have moved on from Lisandro Martinez's explosive post-match comments this week.

Carrick's close friend and team-mate Wayne Rooney led the condemnation of Martinez, saying the Argentine defender could "rip the dressing room apart" with his attack on United's hierarchy after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Former United skippers Roy Keane and Gary Neville have also had their say, among a huge amount of analysis.

Martinez has apologised for the timing of comments, which turned the spotlight on director of football Jason Wilcox, but not for the words themselves.

"There's a lot of people who say a lot of things - ex-pros or not ex-pros - it doesn't necessarily mean they understand what is going on here," said Carrick in his pre-match media conference at United's Carrington training ground.

"Just because people talk on the outside doesn't mean that is the truth. I am telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I have seen it for a while. That is it, plain and simple. We are living it every day and know what it feels like.

"We are emotional and care a lot. Sometimes someone says something that maybe you shouldn't say at that certain time, but it doesn't distract us from what we are creating here and the environment and spirit within the group.

"It [the squad] is not affected, I am telling you."

Carrick confirmed Martinez would be "part of the squad" for Sunday's Premier League trip to Leeds at Elland Road (14:00 BST).

Martinez apologises for outburst and fined by Man Utd

Man Utd a circus after Martinez comments - Keane

Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout

Martinez singled out the 'technical director' for criticism in Madrid.

There was no mention of Wilcox in his statement, although the former Leeds and Blackburn player, who was made United's director of football in the aftermath of Dan Ashworth's sacking in December 2024, was part of the discussions with Martinez that led to his latest statement on his conduct.

Wilcox is back in the spotlight, after also being targeted by Ruben Amorim in his final press conference before his dismissal in January.

The 55-year-old has only spoken publicly once since, to United's own media channel, 12 months ago.

"I don't think it's for me to say whether he should or not," said Carrick, when asked if Wilcox should be the one explaining his actions to the media.

"I've got no problem sitting here, talking to you guys and leading the group, leading the team, leading the football club from this position. We're all in it together.

Carrick does not feel Martinez's failure to mention Wilcox by name is an issue.

"He's released his statement, he's realised he's made a mistake, and I think that's enough for all of us to move on with," he said.

"We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care. There's a way of doing that, and that's already been acknowledged.

"But we need to carry that intensity, that willingness, togetherness and spirit and everything else you can bring with that. As a group, we need to use it, and we've got to use it in the right way."

The negative headlines are the last thing Carrick needed at the present time.

His side go to Leeds on the back of a five-match winless run. United have not gone six games without a victory since the end of the 2018-19 campaign, just after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had been confirmed as permanent manager.

Carrick knows the importance of ending that sequence in terms of easing the pressure on his own future.

However, he refuses to accept that as being crucial.

"I don't need results," he said. "We all need results.

"It's not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual. It is bigger than me, bigger than any player, or anyone else who works at this football club. It always has been.

"I don't go into every day at work in this situation, [ahead of] this game, thinking it's about me. It's really not. It's about the football club; what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to. That's what drives us."

Martinez's outburst was triggered by United's lengthy injury list that led to Ayden Heaven playing at left-back in Madrid.

Cover for Luke Shaw, who missed the game through injury, and Benjamin Sesko were viewed by some as being crucial in the summer.

In addition to Shaw's absence, Sesko is yet to start a Premier League game this season.

The Slovenia forward, a £74m signing from RB Leipzig in August 2025, suffered a recurrence of the shin injury that curtailed his 2025-26 season in last month's EFL Cup defeat by Brighton.

For the third pre-match press conference running, Carrick said he was unable to give a timescale on Sesko's return.

"Ben's kind of still undergoing a couple of checks before we update on timelines," he said.

"We're just trying to be clear with what that looks like but he's still a little bit further away."
