items.title: Doing Nothing Might Be Your Best Recovery Tool – and Now There’s Proof
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Rethink your recovery: Compression, cryotherapy, ice baths, and other costly tools fail to test better than doing nothing in new study.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images)

Toss the compression socks, empty the ice bath, and cancel the recovery ride.

A new study has reinforced the theory that the best way to recover from a hard workout might be …. doing nothing.

No freezing cold-plunge. No $100 cryotherapy session. And definitely no compression socks.

A new study on endurance athletes suggests that sitting on the couch, eating well, and sleeping plenty might be just as effective as any costly, time-consuming recovery modality.

The researchers’ findings should have you rethink how you plan to recover from your next heinous interval session or gravel fondo.

Because while the study doesn’t definitively disprove certain recovery tools, it significantly questions the confidence of the claims used to sell them.

Investing time and money in compression socks, ice baths, cryotherapy sessions, and electrostim devices might be buying you little more than belief.

The premise that “you don’t overtrain, you under-recover” has driven an obsession with recovery hacks among cash-rich, time-poor amateurs who’re chasing easy gains.

Someone’s always selling a new “best way” to dodge DOMS, feel eternally fresh, and hit personal bests, every day.

What’s in the body, what’s in the mind? Was it the 10 hours of sleep or the four-minute cryotherapy session that saw you right after your most recent 100-mile ride?

Beyond that, the science behind many popular recovery tools rests on weak conclusions or is muddled by conflicts of interest.

A new independent paper published in August tries to cut through the noise.

By focusing on well-trained athletes who typically recover better than desk jockeys, it narrows the therapeutic window and reduces the chance for confounders. And unlike any previous review, it reports the certainty of its findings.

Take a breath before you read it: “ Physical recovery modalities in competitive and elite endurance athletes: a systematic review and network meta-analysis finding limited evidence of benefit over passive recovery .”

The study pooled trials of 273 “competitive, elite, or professional” cyclists, runners, swimmers, triathletes, and cross-country skiers. The mixed-sex cohort spanned a range of ages.

And don’t think the findings might not apply to you, dear reader. The minimum VO2 Max score required for inclusion was more than achievable for most athletes who “train” rather than tootle. These weren’t all Tour de France pros and Ironman champions.

Subjects were rated for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness), creatine kinase (a marker of muscle damage), performance restoration, and a number of other recovery markers after they used one or many popular recovery tools.

All the hip recovery modalities, and some old-school favorites, were put to the test.

The study focused on cold-water immersion, cryotherapy, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, massage, compression garments, and active recovery (i.e., an easy ride).

The comparators? Passive recovery (i.e., doing nothing) and, as a sham intervention, immersion in a room-temperature bath.

The experiment’s conclusion is bad news for your trusty compression socks. It doesn’t do much for the burgeoning recovery technology industry, either.

The headline? No recovery tool can claim to be better than doing nothing.

“In competitive and elite endurance athletes, no physical recovery modality has been shown to outperform passive recovery on any outcome we examined,” reads the summary.

“For sport-specific performance, the evidence goes further: compression garments, active recovery, and neuromuscular electrical stimulation can be said, with low to moderate certainty, not to produce a clinically important benefit.”

The study also failed to find any comparative benefit of one recovery method over another. A $100 cryotherapy session might be no better than a 30-minute recovery ride.

But that said, this isn’t the brink of armageddon for ice baths, compression socks, or Ridley Scott-inspired cryotherapy chambers.

The study’s findings are far from conclusive, despite using 47 comparison trials across nearly 300 athletes.

The authors themselves point out several weaknesses in the methodology and complicating factors in the interpretation of the results. Indeed, result certainty was rated “very low” in 31 of the 47 trials comparing a recovery tool vs. doing nothing.

The one “moderate-certainty” finding might raise eyebrows, however. It might also reduce the average sock height in the finishing area of your next gran fondo or post-race flight.

The evidence concluded with reasonable certainty that compression garments – the cheapest, easiest, most accessible recovery modality out there – do not improve performance.

Recovery, however, is not all in the legs.

The placebo effect of any recovery modality is strong.

That’s why, in the science-backed Tour de France, you still see riders shivering in ice baths after a stage and staggering around hotels squeezed into compression socks.

As Tudor Pro Cycling trainer James Spragg once told Velo :

“Some of the things riders use in recovery could also be considered placebos, or aren’t so well-proven. But to be honest, we don’t care if some things in the recovery protocol ‘work’ or not, just as long as riders feel it’s a benefit,” Spragg said.

“If a rider feels more confident for the next day as a result of something in their recovery process, it’s all a benefit,” he added.

As Spragg said, belief is a powerful component of recovery, as it is of performance.

Many studies have found that recovery methods with the most noticeable sensory effect typically have the strongest influence on reported outcomes.

For example, the pressure of a compression sock or the shock of an ice bath might convince athletes they’re primed for PRs in their next workout.

The new paper reinforces the placebo theory by using a room temperature bath as a “sham” intervention.…

items.title: How Red Bull has improved its F1 engine without ADUO
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton is calling it the most powerful engine in Formula 1. Toto Wolff says it's clearly not lagging behind. The FIA has officially labelled it the benchmark.

After Max Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, the paddock consensus is clear that Red Bull’s recent gains have come as much from the power unit as from its chassis.

Yes, the team's Baku upgrade delivered the downforce step and a more consistent aero platform that has put Verstappen in a super happy place with the balance.

But in F1 2026, cars and drivers are nowhere if the power unit is not up to the job – and on this front Red Bull Power Trains (RBPT) is no longer playing clear second fiddle to championship leaders Mercedes.

Telemetry traces and those ghost lap replays have highlighted that Red Bull’s poles have been won as much on the straights as the corners – with a top speed profile that was not there earlier in the year.

As Hamilton said after being unable to challenge Verstappen in the Singapore sprint: “To overtake the most powerful engine on the grid is not so easy.”

What is fascinating about this shift in the battle between power unit manufacturers – where once Mercedes was a step above everyone – is that it has happened without any hardware steps.

While Ferrari has used both of the upgrades it is allowed under the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules, neither Mercedes nor Red Bull has brought any new homologations.

Mercedes is holding fire until at least the United States Grand Prix, while Red Bull can't have anything new because it's been ruled as the benchmark engine (twice) by the FIA’s analysis.

But just because there have been no specification updates doesn't mean Red Bull hasn't unlocked more performance.

The story of its season, and how it's at a point where rivals are admiring what it's doing, is because it's more consistently using the full potential of its power unit.

Like a car's peaky aero package that delivers a lot of downforce in a very narrow window, Red Bull's power unit shone - but not at every track and every lap.

But there was no evidence of that characteristic being there regularly over the first half of the season. Mercedes looked to be in a class of its own.

Looking at how things have changed, RBPT’s technical director Ben Hodgkinson told us the key steps forward are coming from calibration work – which has involved fuel supplier Exxon Mobil and Red Bull's own engineers at Milton Keynes.

This is effectively detailed work to marry up power output, fuel consumption, energy harvesting, and deployment strategies.

“We've sort of found that the most powerful engine that we can create has made a combustion system that is quite challenging to make sure you always get the maximum performance out of it,” Hodgkinson told The Race,

“That's put an awful lot of pressure onto the calibration team to try and make sure that it's always working at that right level.”

The picture at the start of the season of how things looked between Mercedes and Red Bull was also exacerbated by decisions taken at Milton Keynes to hold fire in committing to its design.

It elected to keep developing longer than originally planned. This meant it was still pushing forward with its design when, ideally, it should have been doing the preparation work on durability and calibration.

“At our original point in the pre-season, when we were planning to freeze the spec, we weren't really happy with the performance levels,” said Hodgkinson.

“So we made the decision to just keep going, which was giving us less and less time to do durability runs and do all the calibration work that we needed to do.

“We actually started the season with quite immature calibrations. But they have got better and better throughout every single race.”

Hodgkinson says the improvements have never stopped and there was a “nice step of learning” between the Baku weekend and Sepang – where that maiden RBPT win was delivered.

“This was able to make sure that the engine was performing closer to its best at all times,” he said.

“We sort of have an engine that sometimes underperforms to what we know it can do. There has always been this prize that if you can get it performing at the top of its range for every single lap, we're going to be in a really good place.”

But it's not just understanding the power unit in isolation that Red Bull has made progress this year. The F1 2026 rules have meant power units and chassis are having to work in closer unison than ever before, and this is an area where things have moved a lot at Milton Keynes.

Hodgkinson adds, “There's been a much, much deeper collaboration between the chassis and the PU side.

“It is about how you balance energy and deploy it, where you can harvest it and working with the drivers. I can really see how that team is just getting stronger and stronger. When we win, it really is a one-team victory - evidence of us all coming together.”

Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, plus the pace it showed in Baku, have shown that the Red Bull package is not lacking anywhere.

As Wolff said: “You can’t see that it’s lagging. They have done it very well. The ICE seems to be very competitive. Obviously, you can see that with ADUO, but also in terms of energy recovery and energy deployment there. It’s pretty good.”

Hodgkinson thinks the RBPT is not at its peak yet – with the ever-improving calibration pointing to further gains this year.

“There's still improvement to be had just from the calibration side, so I think that you'll see a bit of that this season,” he said.

And then of course it must not be forgotten that a new fuel flow regime and a change of turbo boost pressure will somewhat reset the power units in 2027.

“What should have been a year of refining things is kind of a year of going again on the combustion system,” said Hodgkison, who sees opportunity for gains even if RBPT remains without any extra ADUO allowances.

“We've learned an awful lot about how to get the best out of this combustion system, and so the changes that we're making for next season are from that learning.”

Hodgkinson is not the sort of person who is happy to rest on his laurels.

“I think there's a lot that could still be got through the calibration,” he said. “I can see our engine; there's still a margin to its theoretical best that we see on dynos.

“And actually, it's not all down to calibration to solve that. You can make some hardware changes that make it a bit easier too, or a bit less of a diva, to try and use some terminology that's often used in F1.

“Our combustion system could be described as a bit of a diva, and we need to make it slightly easier to extract the best out of it.

“So that's some of the changes that we're making for next year, and hopefully we can get a nice step on in performance.”

It is little wonder Mercedes is predicting a tougher title battle than it's had this year.

Wolff said after Singapore: "One thing is for sure: next year it's full-on the fight between the teams and Red Bull is part of that."

items.title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin pips Biesterbos to stage 3 victory after well-placed Paul Magnier unclips during sprint
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Milan Fretin (Cofidis) sped to victory on stage 3 of the Tour of Guangxi, claiming the longest stage of the race in a messy sprint ahead of stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL).

With the finish line on a wide road into Bama, the sprint was spread all across the road with little room for organisation, and most sprinters in the wind early and making a desperate dash for the line.

Powering up the right-hand side of the road, Fretin just held Biesterbos off to claim the win, with Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) grabbing third. Fabio Jakobsen (Visma-Lease a Bike) had his best sprint of the week so far to take fourth.

Stage 1 winner Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) had the best lead-out, dropped off just 150m from the line, but as he opened up his sprint he pulled his right foot out of his pedal and lost all speed. He was swamped by the pack and left banging his handlebars in frustration as he crossed the line in 21st.

Magnier's misfortune and Biesterbos' second place means that the Dutchman now takes over the lead of the race, donning the red jersey on Thursday, though a hilly day on stage 4 means he probably won't hold onto it for long.

Though it finished in a sprint, stage 3 from Jingxi to Bama was an undulating and long 212km day, with four climbs in the final 60km as the difficulty began to ramp up in China.

A three-man breakaway of Jasha Sütterlin (Jayco AlUla), Tobias Bayer (Alpecin-Premier Tech) and Wang Ruidong (China) went away early in the stage, with Wang's efforts in the climbs earning him the KoM jersey.

Despite the profile of the final part of the stage looking ripe for attacks, it wasn't quite as aggressive as it could have been, with the leaders not caught until 20km to go with Wang valiantly pushing on solo to be the final escapee.

From there, Soudal-QuickStep and Decathlon CMA CGM kept the pace high and controlled enough to discourage any attacks and keep things together for their desired bunch sprint – though ultimately both teams got little for their efforts, with Magnier's incident costing him, and Olav Kooij not able to contest the sprint.

The Tour of Guangxi kicks up a notch tomorrow, with four categorised climbs and many more uncategorised ascents on a day that takes in over 2,700m of climbing before a downhill finish into Tian'e.

items.title: The F1 pit stop that helped save lives
items.content: <article>How an F1 pit stop inspired changes to hospital care that have helped save lives ever since.</article>
items.lbText:
When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.

But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.

The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.

At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.

Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.

Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.

As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.

Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.

"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.

"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."

The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.

Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.

Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.

Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.

Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.

Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.

The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.

The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.

F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.

At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.

This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.

David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."

Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.

Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

items.title: Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan Liew
items.author: Jonathan Liew
items.content:
Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club

For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club

H eartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person to scrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season , given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Prime after United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid on Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence.

For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.

But traducing the messenger will always be easier than hearing the message, even if Martínez’s views are widely shared within the United dressing room . If the fallout from the Manchester City legal case has demonstrated anything, it is English football’s ingrained reluctance to scrutinise the owners and executives who hold more influence over the sport than anybody else. Men in boots, not men in suits. Hey, watch the ball. It’s going to move!

All the same, it’s worth parsing exactly what Martínez was complaining about, because it’s a good deal more complex than it may appear on first viewing. Player calls out board – and specifically “technical director” Jason Wilcox – for failing to invest sufficiently in the squad over the summer. This was a summer in which United brought in three midfielders (Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba), a reserve goalkeeper (Karl Darlow), nobody up front and nobody in defence. So far, so simple.

But let’s begin to unpick the threads. Why did United not buy a defender in the summer, despite pursuing deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly? Because they were unable to sell a defender. There was no interest in Diogo Dalot or Noussair Mazraoui, nor in Harry Maguire, nor in Luke Shaw or Martínez, whose contracts are up next summer in any case. This is the product of recruitment decisions made and deals signed years ago. But why do United, one of the world’s most lucrative clubs, need to sell to buy in the first place?

Perhaps for the same reason they baulked at the asking price for Elliot Anderson and decided to sign the inconsistent Santos and the adequate but overpromoted Tielemans instead: this is a club in austerity measures, whose part-owner Jim Ratcliffe has been furiously cutting costs and raising ticket prices, determined to curb the years of excess that preceded him, where mediocre players were signed on ridiculous money, where failing coaches were paid to leave. But why would United, one of the most commercially successful clubs in footballing history, ever need to cut costs?

Perhaps as a result of the more than £1bn drained out of the club by the Glazers in their 21 years of ownership, not just in dividends but share sales and interest payments on the debt they undertook to buy the club, while neglecting the maintenance of Old Trafford and the training ground at Carrington. Whether he knows it or not, when Martínez is criticising the lack of investment he is in effect holding the Glazers accountable for more than two decades of avarice and mismanagement.

All of which lends a certain significance to Martínez’s intervention that goes beyond the churn of the weekly news cycle. Has any serving United player spoken out so frankly about the ruins of the Glazer ownership? Ole Gunnar Solskjær made a minor stand in early 2005, before they had arrived at the club. Cristiano Ronaldo threw some hand grenades over his shoulder a few days before he left for the second time in 2022. Countless others waited for the safety of retirement, when their disgruntlement could be monetised for personal gain, rather than used to stigmatise them, as Martínez will doubtless be stigmatised in the coming days.

Does any of this help United to win games in the short term? Almost certainly not. Martínez attempted to clarify his comments in a social media post on Wednesday night. He may still be dispatched to the bomb squad anyway, for the crime of pointing out that the emperor secured his throne almost entirely through the use of payment-in-kind loans.

Inevitably Michael Carrick too will be gone before long, away to the great Overlap podcast in the sky. A few months ago I wrote hopefully that Carrick might be the ideal man to cut through the noise and nonsense. I was wrong. The noise has beaten him; the nonsense always wins; any accumulated credit from last season has long since evaporated.

Of course it’s not Carrick’s fault that United haven’t signed a new defender in almost two years, that Bruno Fernandes is so clearly playing through discomfort, that Joshua Zirkzee is still somehow hanging around the place, that the ownership decided to embark on a purge of season-ticket holders in the summer, generating a huge wave of ill-feeling and apathy that can be felt at Old Trafford on matchdays: an entire fanbase trying to work out whether they actually still care about this.…

items.title: Preseason Game Preview: Knicks vs. Raptors, October 15, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks host the Raptors (2-1) Thursday at Madison Square Garden in the final preseason game for both.  Revenge? Do preseason scrimmages matter enough to call this a revenge game? Winning would be nice, though. The world champs have dropped all four of their preseason games, with the worst game of the bunch coming on Tuesday in Toronto. 

On the second night of a back-to-back, coach Mike Brown rested his starters and the reserves suffered a 50-point beating. Kawhi Leonard (in his first game since rejoining the Raps) scored 21 points in 17 minutes. Scottie Barnes added 19 points, six rebounds and four assists. Collin Murray-Boyles dropped 19 and nine. RJ Barrett had 17. James Wiseman led New York with 18 points and 10 rebounds while the rest of the team struggled to stay in their shorts. 

The takeaway? When Toronto plays its actual rotation and New York does not, the gap is wide.

Toronto is built with two-way versatility and physicality up front. With Leonard and Barnes on the wing, and Barrett and Immanuel Quickley in the backcourt, they have enough talent to be a problem. Jakob Poeltl anchors the paint and remains a serviceable center.

New York has spent the preseason evaluating depth pieces and managing minutes for the starters. Tonight will be the last dress rehearsal before they uncork their season on Tuesday. We assume that means the starters will play a little longer, as they get back into full game shape, and Mike Brown will use this time to get last looks at the guys hovering on the edge of the roster. Prediction? Another L to run the table, of course!

UPDATE (10:35 a.m.): Drew Eubanks has sustained a torn pectoral muscle and will be out indefinitely. That’s a tough break for the center, who was Wiseman’s primary competition for the third-string spot.

Who: New York Knicks (0-4) at Toronto Raptors (2-1)Date: Tuesday, October 15, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, NYCFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky
